items.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite new optimism
items.description: The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader’s misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country. Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message “Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!” But given everything that’s happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner? The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all? Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship. Just listen to the way they talk about each other. “Zelensky’s not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump told Newsmax last week. The verbal assault has continued this week. “Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader’s suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history. Such personal attacks are typical of Trump’s sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It’s hard to know when to take them seriously. In June, he lashed out at Israel’s prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu “has no f**king judgement”. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a “great warrior prime minister”. “Trump can always do another U-turn,” says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. “But this does look bad.” For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart. But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of “decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends” and voiced the fear that “some political decision has been made to slow down support for us.” Answering Trump’s charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever. “We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity,” he wrote on Telegram on Monday. But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship? In some ways, we’ve been here before. After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of “gambling with World War III”, the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing. The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead. One exception, in the wake of this year’s US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles. Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said “only a couple” of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine’s stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks. Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv. Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump’s all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel. Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine’s campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington’s willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv. Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin. “What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians,” former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC. “It’s inexplicable and saddening.” Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it “an important and truly historic moment”. For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the “spirit of Alaska”, a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025. Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine’s access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service. Amid an escalation in Russia’s drone and missile war on Ukraine’s cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking. “We didn’t receive it during ballistic attacks for three days,” Zelensky told NBC News. On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded. The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a “software problem” for the temporary lack of early warnings. Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine’s access to Starlink. A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine’s military to intercept fast moving Russian drones. Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones. It’s not clear where any order to limit Ukraine’s use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House. Rubio said “no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet.” But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations. Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump’s seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole – and Zelensky in particular. A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine. When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump’s demands that he investigate charges of election interference. During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused. At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump’s first impeachment. Whether Trump’s resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it’s clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip. Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin. Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped “to straighten out a few things.” “There’s nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago,” he said diplomatically. Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink. “I think we will have good results too,” he said. Yet despite the optimistic tone, it’s hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

items.title: Cameroun : la première journée mondiale de la santé environnementale célébrée à Yaoundé
items.description: © DR Célébrée pour la première fois le 19 octobre 2026 au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé, la Journée mondiale de la santé environnementale a placé la science au cœur de la protection des communautés face à la pollution et à la dégradation des écosystèmes. Une première aux accents d'alerte. Le Cameroun a célébré pour la première fois, le 19 octobre 2026 au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé, la Journée mondiale de la santé environnementale, sous le thème : "la santé environnementale : s'appuyer sur la science pour protéger les communautés". Habituellement célébrée le 26 septembre depuis 2011, cette journée vise à sensibiliser décideurs, professionnels et grand public au rôle déterminant de la santé environnementale dans la prévention des maladies. Au Cameroun, le lien est direct. La santé publique est impactée par la dégradation des écosystèmes, la gestion inappropriée des déchets et leur brûlage sauvage qui libère des toxines, la pollution de l'air à Douala et Yaoundé où les particules fines franchissent les seuils de sécurité, et l'insalubrité de l'eau. Les conséquences sont lourdes : maladies hydriques, affections respiratoires, prolifération des vecteurs. Les formations sanitaires reçoivent chaque jour enfants, mères et travailleurs souffrant de toux chronique, d'asthme sévère et d'infections aiguës causées par les émissions des transports et les poussières. Face à cela, le Gouvernement applique la stratégie "une seule santé". Parmi les actions concrètes : déploiement massif d'un réseau de surveillance de la qualité de l'air en temps réel via des stations fixes et mobiles, renforcement des contrôles et inspections environnementales, et soutien aux acteurs de terrain et municipalités à travers des initiatives de salubrité publique. Présidant la cérémonie, le Ministre de l'Environnement a appelé à la responsabilité de tous : collectivités, société civile, médias et secteur privé doivent respecter la législation environnementale. Aux citoyens, il a lancé un appel simple : "ne pas jeter d'ordures dans les drains, planter un arbre, préserver nos cours d'eau, l'arrêt définitif des feux de poubelles". Cet article Cameroun : la première journée mondiale de la santé environnementale célébrée à Yaoundé est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Ogun suspends Eselu over alleged partisan politics
items.description: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Ogun State Government has suspended the Eselu of Iselu Kingdom in Yewa North Local Government Area, Oba Akintunde Akinyemi, with immediate effect over alleged involvement in partisan political activities. The suspension was approved by the State Executive Council pursuant to Section 52(1) of the Ogun State Obas and Chiefs Law, 2021, pending a detailed investigation into the allegations against the monarch. The decision was conveyed in a letter dated October 20, 2026, signed by the Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Hon. Ganiyu Hamzat. According to the letter, the council acted following several complaints about the monarch’s conduct, particularly his alleged involvement in overtly partisan political activities, some of which were reportedly publicised by him. The government said partisan political activities by traditional rulers were contrary to customary law and prohibited by statute, warning that such conduct could undermine the dignity of the traditional institution and threaten peaceful coexistence among residents with different political affiliations. It added that the suspension was in the interest of peace, order and good governance in the state, particularly in Iselu Kingdom, while the allegations were subjected to an official investigation. As part of the conditions of the suspension, Oba Akinyemi was directed to vacate the palace and refrain from entering it throughout the period of his suspension. He was also instructed not to present himself as, or claim recognition as, the Eselu of Iselu Kingdom. The government further prohibited him from wearing or using any crown, whether beaded or otherwise, ileke, beaded staff, irukere or other paraphernalia associated with the office of an Oba during the suspension. The letter also directed the monarch to make himself available promptly for any meeting or sitting convened by the state government to investigate the allegations against him. Copies of the letter were sent to the Secretary of Yewa North Local Government and the Commissioner of Police, Ogun State Command, for their information and necessary action. The post Ogun suspends Eselu over alleged partisan politics appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The Contradictions of Troy Jackson
items.description: The clouds, piled in a dark heap over the Blueberry Ridge mobile-home park in Wells, Maine, looked like they would open up any minute. Residents sat in neatly arranged folding chairs behind a double-wide trailer, waiting for Troy Jackson, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, to appear. Meanwhile, campaign staffers buzzed around like hornets out of a nest, freshly kicked. I was seated at the periphery, flanked on the left by two pockmarked fake deer—3-D archery targets—and on the right by an elderly chain-smoker who politely angled her cigarette away from me as she talked. She told me that she didn’t know much about Jackson but was going to knock on doors for him anyway. “He seems like he’s down-to-earth,” she said. “That he’s one of us.” Jackson is one of them. He’s a fifth-generation logger born to a 16-year-old high-school dropout, and, as he is fond of repeating, he grew up as a “poor kid in a town full of poor kids.” At one time, he lived in a mobile home. A slick banner on his campaign website declares: Mainer By Birth. Logger By Trade. Senator for the People . I’d come to Blueberry Ridge to see Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner as the nominee in July, after Platner resigned due to multiple scandals. The park was bought by a real-estate-investment company in 2021, and a group of residents has claimed that the new owners have made life there more expensive and worse. Now the group is pushing for a rent cap, and Jackson was there over Labor Day weekend to show support. When he addressed the crowd, his voice was measured but tinged with what sounded like genuine frustration. “The greed that’s happening right now in this country, that people in mobile-home parks are feeling, is like something I’ve never seen,” he said. Jackson marveled at a mason jar of muddy tap water that got passed around, apparent evidence of the park’s deteriorating living conditions. He seemed to be in his element, and after the event was over, he stayed to shake hands and talk about the travails of mobile-home life until his staffers pulled him away. [ Read: One morning of controlled chaos in Maine ] The next stop on his tour that day was People’s Inclusive Welding, a school in South Portland whose mission is to provide a “safe and supportive environment for underserved and underrepresented communities to learn a skilled trade.” There, Jackson watched a torch demonstration, surrounded by the language of hyper-progressivism: a metal slab emblazoned with the text WHAT’S YOUR SAFE WORD? ; a door covered in dozens of stickers with radical messages ( SOLIDARITY MEANS WEARING A MASK and DESTROY ALL BORDERS ); a gigantic mural, painted the colors of the trans flag, proclaiming BLM and ACAB —an abbreviation for “All Cops Are Bastards.” He seemed to instinctively edge away from the mural as a local-news outlet snapped photos of him. The contrast between these two events—one at a trailer park populated mostly by retirees, the other at a shop catering to progressive urban tradespeople—reflects the tensions in the Jackson campaign as a whole. Jackson seems to be attempting to pair a left-leaning, economically populist package with “woke” cultural ideals, which working-class voters tend to reject. Jackson’s unsuccessful run for governor earlier this year was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America and Bernie Sanders, who affirmed his support for Jackson’s Senate bid and has appeared at campaign events on his behalf. Several labor unions have also endorsed Jackson. He supports Medicare for All, bans on congressional stock trading, tax cuts for workers, and tax hikes for billionaires. He also favors restricting assault weapons and abolishing ICE. As a state senator, he voted in favor of trans women being housed in women’s prisons, and of qualified trans teens receiving treatments such as hormone therapy without parental consent; he voted against a ban on trans women’s participation on women’s sports teams. In 2023, he co-sponsored legislation to allow later-term abortions after fetal viability. On economic issues, Jackson is in sync with the working-class and rural voters he says he is championing. Sixty-three percent of Americans without a college degree and 76 percent of those who make less than $50,000 a year say that the government should be responsible for ensuring health-care coverage, for example. On cultural matters, however, Jackson is out of step with many of those he claims to be giving a voice to. Most Americans without a college degree say that protecting gun rights is more important than gun control, and that guns make the country safer. These Americans are also more likely than college graduates to express negative views about illegal immigration. Likewise, a majority of people making less than $50,000 a year or who did not go to college say that abortion is morally unacceptable, whereas those making more than $100,000 or who did go to college say the opposite. On gender identity, majorities of Americans without a four-year college degree say that gender transitions are morally wrong, that trans people should play on sports teams that match their birth sex, and that being trans is not an innate condition but is instead caused by social factors. Similar trends play out in Maine, where people without a four-year college degree are more likely than people with a degree to view illegal immigration as a serious problem, and where trans women’s participation in women’s sports is unpopular across the electorate. (I asked the Jackson campaign for an interview so that he could elaborate on his views, but it refused multiple requests.) Despite its down-home signifiers and KICKING ASS FOR THE WORKING CLASS T-shirts, the Jackson campaign’s pairing of leftist economic populism with progressive cultural stances fits seamlessly into the broader professional-class insurgency roiling the Democratic Party. This movement, which some have referred to as a Democratic “tea party,” appears animated by a theory of persuasion that one might call “left maximalism.” The tacit wager of left maximalists, including Jackson, seems to be that enough working-class voters will stomach unpopular left-wing cultural policies provided that a candidate also supports popular left-wing economic positions. This strategy has shown some signs of success lately, as evidenced by the DSA-endorsed candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier’s surprise primary win in New York City’s Thirteenth Congressional District, one of the poorest in the state. She managed to unseat an incumbent establishment opponent despite arguing that deportations are wrong under any circumstance and that national borders and prisons should be abolished—views that are not exactly common among the working class. Similarly, before Platner’s collapse, he used a left-maximalist approach to win his primary. It remains to be seen, however, whether left maximalism will fly as a general-election strategy in Maine. Winning will require Jackson to hold together a coalition that includes both college-educated residents of prosperous coastal cities and towns, and the rural, socially moderate, working-class voters Democrats have been alienating in recent years. The frictions in the Jackson campaign’s platform call to mind the work of Daniel Bell, a mid-20th-century sociologist who once described himself as “a socialist in economics, a liberal in politics, and a conservative in culture.” In his 1976 book, The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism , Bell argued that capitalism had started to undermine itself. As Bell observed, capitalism took root in the United States during the 19th and early-20th centuries, when the country’s social life was defined by puritanical moralism and the Protestant work ethic. Americans saved money, prioritized the public good, toiled mostly without complaint, and were disinclined to acquisitiveness. But after World War II, he wrote, thrift and public spiritedness were displaced by consumerist individualism, which focused on permissiveness, pleasure, and the self. Writing during a decade of economic crisis and high inflation, Bell warned that unfettered capitalism would weaken important institutions, cultural values, and social bonds—and ultimately lead to a society as unstable as it was selfish. If Bell was right to spotlight the “cultural contradictions of capitalism” in the 1970s, the cultural contradictions of anti-capitalism may well prove to be one of the most potent political conundrums of the 2020s: The American left has produced an environment that alienates many working-class people from candidates espousing economics designed to benefit them. [ Read: Why do rich kids love socialism? ] Jackson, apparently trying to manage these contradictions, is acting as though he can be everything to everyone. One minute, his team is launching a folksy ad , set at a backyard barbecue, about loggers paying more taxes than billionaires. The next minute, the campaign is dropping a side-eye-emoji’d social-media clip of the candidate sassily sipping boba tea beside a Pride flag. Depending on your perspective, this mishmash is reflective either of a politician who is trying to represent all Mainers, or of a man whose cultural politics sit uneasily alongside those of the working-class electorate—not to mention his own past beliefs. When Jackson first (and unsuccessfully) ran for state office in 2000, he did so as a Republican . By 2002, he was an independent, and by 2004, a Democrat. Yet even after changing his party affiliation, he voted against same-sex-marriage legislation in 2009, and received a perfect score from an anti-abortion group, Maine Right to Life, in 2010. By 2017, though, Jackson had done an about- face . He eventually began receiving accolades from pro-choice organizations for his support of abortion rights. Jackson, who was raised Catholic, has described abortion as an issue he has long wrestled with, and has said that he was simply persuaded that his prior views were wrong. It is more than possible that Jackson’s pivot did come from a sincere change of heart, rather than from a cynical calculation about the concessions necessary to succeed as a Democrat. And the mixed messages of Jackson’s current campaign are not irreconcilable. Jackson can court the Rural Flannel-Wearing Tree Cutters and the Urban Boba Wokes at the same time, and perhaps he really will win enough of each for the Maine electoral math to work out in the Democrats’ favor. Polling shows a tight race, and the Iran quagmire, Donald Trump’s subbasement approval rating, and rising heating-oil prices in advance of the Maine winter are unlikely to do his opponent, the five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins, any favors. But what may work as a matter of immediate tactics is not necessarily a strategy for fundamentally reshaping the demographics of the Democratic Party within the state, or outside it. Cultural politics, not economic politics, are the left’s primary barrier to winning back the working class. Left maximalists tend to treat the working class as a junior partner rather than as their primary constituency. Progressive urban professionals may get the economic and social politics they want, while rural and working-class voters are asked to compromise their moral and cultural belief system in exchange for promises of health care and an increased minimum wage. [ Read: The blockbuster that captured a growing American rift ] After Jackson departed Blueberry Ridge, I stuck around the backyard to talk with some residents. One was a union tinsmith and lifelong Democrat who told me he doesn’t care about culture-war issues and is more worried about how labor is being fleeced. Another was a tollbooth worker and three-time Trump voter who was dismayed that the president he’d voted for had done so little for the little people. He seemed ready for something different, and sympathized with Troy Jackson’s anti-corporate politics, but said that he could never vote for Jackson because of his stances on immigration and gender issues. Progressives may wonder why a Mainer whose trailer park is allegedly being wrecked by an investment firm would care more about immigration policy than affordability issues as he decides which candidate to support. But one could also ask the opposite question: Why are highly educated leftists, and politicians such as Jackson who appeal to them, often unwilling to give even an inch on social issues? If socialists and populists—even blue-collar leftists such as Jackson—are so wedded to progressivism that they do not compromise with the working class, the question is not simply whether such a left can win. The question is whether it truly remains left at all.

items.title: Canadian Officers Don’t Want to Serve in the U.S. Anymore
items.description: T he shortest flight path from Russia to the United States would take an enemy bomber over the North Pole and across Canadian airspace. During the Cold War, that simple fact was the impetus for the creation of the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which forged an integrated radar network across the two countries, effectively treating North American airspace as a single defensive zone. Today, there’s less concern about a Russian barrage landing on U.S. soil, but NORAD remains relevant. Russian bombers still fly near Alaska and the Canadian Arctic. China’s expanding nuclear arsenal poses its own threat. Other airborne objects require vigilance, a lesson underscored by the mysterious flight path, in 2023, of a Chinese spy balloon, which NORAD shot down. This should matter to President Trump, who has identified the Western Hemisphere as a security priority. He even has a name for his approach: the “Donroe Doctrine.” But all is not well at NORAD, the world’s only binational military command, headquartered at the Peterson Space Force Base in Colorado Springs. NORAD, which was founded in 1958, now demonstrates how the president’s disdain for U.S. allies risks undermining the military cooperation that has kept the United States safe for decades. Positions at NORAD and other integrated combatant commands in the United States used to be plum posts for ambitious Canadian military officers, giving them a chance to coordinate with Americans on intelligence, air and missile defense, and joint operations. That’s changing. U.S. and Canadian officials told me that Canada has lately struggled to find senior officers willing to take the jobs, a problem acute enough that Canadian officers have shared their concerns with counterparts in Colorado Springs, Ottawa, and Washington. The reasons are threefold, according to current and former officials who described the dynamic to me on the condition of anonymity in order to address a sensitive subject. Although the influence and sophistication of the U.S. military once made the postings desirable to ambitious officers, some now fear that time in the United States might hurt their chances for future promotions if relations spiral further out of control. They also see diminishing returns from a posting in which they’re likely to have their access curtailed as a byproduct of political tensions. And they face resistance from their families, who worry that anti-Canadian sentiment whipped up by Trump might make the country inhospitable, even temporarily. Canadian officers considering U.S.-based posts don’t believe that they’ll be treated as equals, according to several who spoke with me. While the Trump administration has bullied and threatened numerous allies, these officers perceive particular hostility toward Canada—in part because of the vehemence of the trade dispute, and in part because Prime Minister Mark Carney has been willing, at times, to stand up to Trump. “If you’re a two-star general in Canada, and you’ve got maybe one or two extremely important jobs left in your career, will you use one of them to take up a position in the States, where you might be underemployed, with little access and little meaningful work to show for it?” one Canadian officer asked. [ Read: Trump is learning that his bullying has consequences ] Some of the officials I spoke with noted that strained relations had not yet caused a tactical breakdown—no one had taken their eye off radar scopes or infrared cameras. And that’s what a NORAD spokesperson emphasized in response to my questions, issuing a statement saying that high-level Canadian roles at the binational command “remain fully staffed and highly regarded as career-enhancing opportunities, with Canadian personnel and their families fully integrated and operating with the systemic access required to execute binational defense operations for the homelands.” The true impact of Canadian reluctance to serve in the United States may become manifest only in a crisis. In addition to the essential national-security functions performed by NORAD, the command also fosters camaraderie between the ranks of the two militaries. That’s vital if the U.S. military should ever need to project force to the north, including by moving personnel across Canada. Several of the people I spoke with raised the prospect of a conflict with China, which would quickly threaten Alaska, a crucial strategic hub. Moving U.S. forces to the noncontiguous state would depend on Canadian cooperation. In such a situation, Washington would want Canadian commanders who have served in the United States, so that American officers aren’t building new partnerships but are depending on people they’ve known for years. Canadian generals who’ve passed on postings in the United States because of friction between the two countries are much less likely to be sympathetic. S ince he returned to power last year , Trump has alienated longtime allies while praising rogue states such as North Korea. He has called Germany a “broken country” and said that French President Emmanuel Macron “always gets it wrong.” As a group, European leaders earned the epithet “weak.” He has imposed steep tariffs on their countries and threatened a foundation of Western security by raising doubts about U.S. fidelity to Article 5 of the NATO charter—that an attack on one is an attack on all. Still, when I speak with senior officers in various allied countries—even Denmark , where the armed forces prepared for a possible U.S. invasion of Greenland, earlier this year—they maintain that military-to-military cooperation continues despite political disagreements. Canada may be the first place where that is cracking. “The day-to-day relationship has deteriorated,” David Perry, an Ottawa-based defense analyst, told me. “There’s been a tangible change in the way the two countries interact on defense and security.” That Washington is now choosing to alienate its northern neighbor is ironic because Canada, like other NATO members, is in the process of investing in the type of hard power that will make it an even more useful ally. When I met with Canada’s defense minister, David McGuinty, in February, the government had just released its first defense–industrial strategy, a plan to get weapons faster and—given geopolitical strife—to get more of them from Canadian suppliers. “Obviously continuing to work with the U.S.,” McGuinty said, “but now much more expansively looking to diversify.” Earlier this year, the Canadian government promised to review whether to move forward with a full order of F-35 stealth fighters, which are produced by Lockheed Martin. This month, the government paused its acquisition of U.S.-made Black Hawk helicopters because of trade and diplomatic friction with Washington, according to CBC News and Radio-Canada. Canada is spending billions to upgrade radars, sensors, and other systems. Its participation in Trump’s proposed “Golden Dome” would extend and strengthen the defensive shield, with the potential to protect both countries. But it’s hard to put much faith in protection from a bully. “Trust is easy to lose and hard to build,” Christopher Sands, the director of the Center for U.S.-Canada Studies at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies, told me. The current rancor is entirely different from past trade disputes, which have often been combative—“like a courtroom drama,” Sands said. But the fighting once stayed out of public view, managed by low-profile diplomats. Now the public is in the audience and can’t look away from the president’s antics, which have “poisoned people-to-people relations.” The armed forces couldn’t remain immune forever. A n executive order on Trump’s first day back in office, in January 2025, made Canadian officers wonder whether the U.S. military might be used against them. The order assigned U.S. Northern Command, which shares NORAD’s Colorado headquarters, to the mission to “seal the borders and maintain the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security of the United States.” It did not specify the southern border, causing Canadian officials in Colorado to ask their counterparts, as relations worsened over time: Are you planning to militarize the northern border, one of the world’s longest undefended and peaceful frontiers? U.S. officials tried to reassure them that any action would be cooperative. But the guarantee of cooperation became difficult to sustain. Defending new tariffs imposed on Canada in February 2025, Trump wrote on social media that “Canada ceases to exist as a viable Country” without U.S. support. “Therefore, Canada should become our Cherished 51st State.” Early on, references to Canadian statehood had elicited laughs during staff meetings at NORAD. But the mood soon changed. In April, Trump rebuffed the suggestion that his talk of annexation was just bluster. “I’m really not trolling,” he said in an interview with Time . By the end of the year, jokes within the binational command about the 51st state were met with silence or curt rebuttals. Attitudes had shifted dramatically. An Angus Reid Institute poll found that almost half of Canadians said that their government should view the United States as an “enemy” or “potential threat,” while only 27 percent called Washington a friend and ally. Canadian officers serving in the United States divulged to colleagues that their families didn’t want to visit them over the holidays, because they were afraid of crossing the border or encountering animosity in American communities. In addition to the joint command in Colorado Springs, Canadian generals have served as deputy commanders of U.S. Army corps in North Carolina, Texas, and Washington State. In early 2026, Carney named the dynamic generated by Trump’s hostility to American allies. “We are in the midst of a rupture,” he said, calling on the world’s middle powers to band together to resist bullying and defend international institutions. (Later, in an interview with The New York Times , Carney said that it would have been “irresponsible” not to take into consideration the possibility that Trump might use force against Canada.) [ Watch: How did Trump’s trade fight with Canada go so sideways? ] The president’s insults might have been dismissed as a rhetorical feint—a way to demand better trading terms or shake loose more military spending—but the scorn for Canada was echoed by senior Pentagon leaders. In May, Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy, used social media to complain about Canada’s military readiness and announce that the Trump administration was pausing its participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, a bilateral advisory body to coordinate security policy. “A strong Canada that prioritizes hard power over rhetoric benefits us all,” Colby wrote. “Unfortunately, Canada has failed to make credible progress on its defense commitments.” The board hadn’t met since 2024, so the move was mostly symbolic. But Colby’s withering review prompted nervous questions inside NORAD: Who is this guy, and how much power does he have? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s approach was even less subtle. In August, he posted a photo of two young female Canadian cadets. Their physical appearance seemed not to impress him; he captioned the photo “this is real.” The post stunned Canadians for its crassness and unprofessionalism. Wayne Eyre, who served as chief of Canada’s defense staff from 2021 to 2024, told me that he found Hegseth’s intervention “highly insulting.” It was followed, the next month, by a cartoon image that Trump circulated on his Truth Social feed of him beating Carney with a hockey stick—“unimaginable conduct by the president of the United States, even in our most dystopian imagination,” as one Canadian official put it to me. U.S. military leaders at NORAD have tried to put on a brave face, reporting to visitors that binational cooperation is continuing unimpeded. But away from the spotlight, Canadian officers will acknowledge the strain, current and former officials told me. Eyre warned that cooperation of the kind that he helped oversee is more vulnerable than it might appear. “It’s sad, disappointing, and disturbing to see that deep relationship come under attack,” he said. “In my view, it’s a case of the U.S. undergoing self-harm by discarding and calling into question its competitive advantage, which is this system of alliances.” Most of what the public knows about NORAD comes from its Santa Tracker , a lighthearted simulation of Santa Claus’s journey around the world on Christmas Eve. That’s because the command’s real business—guarding the skies—is mostly invisible. That is, until it stops working.

Coopération Camerou-Royaume Uni : le MINPMEESA mobilise de nouveaux partenariats pour la filière bois
items.description: © DR Le ministre Achille Bassilekin III a reçu le conseiller principal forêts du Royaume-Uni, Neil Scotland. Au menu : transformation locale du bois, développement des PME forestières et valorisation durable des ressources, avec en vitrine le SMEs Wood's Park de Lomié. Yaoundé veut verdir sa diplomatie économique. Le Ministre des Petites et Moyennes Entreprises, de l'Économie Sociale et de l'Artisanat, Achille Bassilekin III, a accordé une audience à M. Neil Scotland, Conseiller principal pour les forêts au ministère britannique des Affaires étrangères, du Commonwealth et du Développement (FCDO). Il était accompagné de Mme Samantha Smith, Haut-Commissaire adjointe et Chargée d'Affaires, et de M. Euan McCarthy, Conseiller régional en climat et environnement pour l'Afrique centrale. Au cœur des échanges : le renforcement de la coopération bilatérale en faveur de la transformation locale du bois, du développement des PME forestières, de la modernisation des équipements, du transfert de technologies et de la mobilisation de financements adaptés aux entreprises camerounaises. Une priorité pour le gouvernement camerounais qui entend faire de la valorisation responsable des ressources forestières un levier de croissance, de compétitivité et de développement durable. Cette dynamique trouve une illustration concrète dans le SMEs Wood's Park de Lomié, dont la convention de partenariat entre le MINPMEESA et la Commune de Lomié a été signée le 6 octobre 2026. Ce projet vise à favoriser le développement des PME, des artisans et des organisations de l'économie sociale, tout en stimulant la création d'emplois et la production de biens à plus forte valeur ajoutée. À travers ces perspectives de coopération, le MINPMEESA entend affirmer son crédo : pour des PME plus compétitives et une transformation locale créatrice de valeur, au bénéfice des entreprises et de l'économie nationale. items.title: NAFDAC to test non-US-made donated drugs, vaccines under Nigeria-US deal
items.description: …. Deploys tracking technology to monitor medical supplies, assures Nigerians of safety checks By Chioma Obinna The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) has said all donated medicines and vaccines under the Nigeria-United States government agreement that are not manufactured in the US will undergo testing for quality, safety and efficacy, amid efforts to bridge the gap in HIV/AIDS treatment supplies following the exit of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). The agency, in a press statementsigned by its Director-General, Prof. Mojisola Christianah Adeyeye, said it would also deploy its technology-driven Track and Trace system to monitor the distribution of all medical products supplied under the United States Government-Nigeria Government (USG-GoN) agreement. NAFDAC explained that US-manufactured products approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, FDA, could benefit from expedited approval under its existing regulatory-reliance framework, owing to the stringent regulatory processes applied by the American agency. It, however, stressed that the arrangement would not strip Nigeria of its authority to regulate medicines and vaccines entering the country. “NAFDAC retains its responsibility for Nigeria’s own decision,” the agency stated, adding that products not manufactured in the United States would be tested for quality, safety and efficacy. The clarification comes as the Nigerian government-backed medical supplies are expected to help sustain HIV/AIDS interventions following the withdrawal of USAID support. NAFDAC said regulatory reliance was intended to reduce unnecessary duplication and accelerate access to quality-assured medical products, not to weaken the country’s regulatory safeguards. The agency cited the position of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Ali Pate, that regulatory reliance does not remove NAFDAC’s authority to evaluate applications, inspect products and manufacturing facilities, conduct risk-based testing, release vaccine lots and undertake post-market surveillance where necessary. According to the agency, the USG-GoN memorandum of understanding refers to its existing regulatory-reliance arrangement with the US FDA, under which products manufactured in the US and approved by the regulator may receive expedited consideration. NAFDAC maintained that it would continue to exercise its statutory responsibility over medicines, vaccines and diagnostics, regardless of the regulatory pathway applied. To demonstrate its commitment to safety, the agency recalled that all COVID-19 vaccines supplied to Nigeria during the pandemic were tested at its Vaccine, Biologics and Medical Devices Laboratory in Yaba, Lagos, despite having been declared safe by the World Health Organisation. It also disclosed that antiretroviral, tuberculosis and malaria drugs supplied through the Global Fund are tested annually by NAFDAC. The agency said these measures reflected its continued commitment to ensuring that essential medicines and vaccines supplied through international partnerships meet the required standards. Beyond product testing and regulatory approval, NAFDAC said it would use the GS1 technology-driven Track and Trace system to monitor the movement and distribution of medical products supplied under the Nigeria-US agreement. The agency explained that the system was used to monitor the distribution of COVID-19 vaccines during the pandemic, with the information preserved in its Traceability Information System, TIS. It added that the system had since been extended to non-COVID-19 vaccines, narcotics, maternal health supplies and newborn-care commodities. “NAFDAC will use the same GS1 technology-driven Track and Trace system to monitor ALL medical products that come into the country under the USG-GoN Agreement,” the statement said. The technology is intended to improve visibility across the medical supply chain and enable the agency to monitor the distribution of products within the country. Reaffirming its commitment to public health, NAFDAC said it would not abdicate its statutory duty to protect Nigerians from unsafe or substandard medical products. “As the Agency with the mandate to safeguard the health of Nigerians, NAFDAC will NOT fail to carry out this responsibility as enshrined in the mandate,” the statement declared. The agency urged the public to be assured that regulatory oversight, appropriate product testing and technology-driven distribution monitoring would remain central to its handling of medical products entering the country under the USG-GoN agreement. The post NAFDAC to test non-US-made donated drugs, vaccines under Nigeria-US deal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tour du Faso 2026 : Dix étapes, huit régions et une quinzaine de nations au départ
items.description: La 37e édition du Tour international cycliste du Faso se tiendra du 30 octobre au 8 novembre 2026. À quelques jours du début de la course, le comité d'organisation a rendu public, ce mercredi 21 octobre 2026, le circuit qui se décline en dix étapes traversant huit régions du Burkina Faso. Les régions concernées sont le Kadiogo, le Koulsé, le Nando, le Bankui, le Guiriko, le Nakambé, le Nazinon et l'Oubri. Le parcours s'ouvre le 30 octobre avec la première étape, Ouagadougou-Kaya. La deuxième mène les coureurs de Ouagadougou à Koudougou, avant la troisième, Koudougou-Boromo. La quatrième étape se dispute sur un circuit fermé à Bobo-Dioulasso, puis la cinquième relie Bobo-Dioulasso à Pâ. La sixième étape conduira le peloton de Saponé à Léo, la septième de Ouagadougou à Pô, et la huitième de Ouagadougou à Koupéla. La neuvième étape mènera de Tenkodogo à Ziniaré, avant l'arrivée finale, le 9 novembre, entre Dapélogo et Ouagadougou. Le Burkina Faso, pays hôte, alignera trois équipes : une sélection nationale et deux équipes régionales. Au total, 21 coureurs burkinabè ont été retenus. Toutes les équipes ont confirmé leur participation. 13 formations prendront part à cette édition 2026 : le Burkina Faso, le Mali, le Niger, la Belgique, le Maroc, le Ghana, le Bénin, le Cameroun, la Côte d'Ivoire, les Pays-Bas, l'Algérie, le Rwanda et l'Afrique du Sud. items.title: Cameroun : le MRC remonté contre Times TV, la chaîne de télévision présente des excuses
items.description: © DR La chaîne de télévision présente ses excuses au Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun qui a exprimé son indignation face aux propos tenus par Serge Olama et Willy Mengue sur les antennes de ladite chaîne. Entre le Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun et Times TV, le climat s’oriente vers l’apaisement après le cri de colère du parti politique lancé le mardi 20 octobre. Le MRC a condamné dans un communiqué la complaisance de la chaine de télévision marquée par l’invitation de Willy Mengue ancien militant exclu du parti et l’absence de recadrage de ce dernier ainsi que de Serge Olama invité pour sa part en septembre. Ce dernier a, rappelle le parti présidé par Tiriane Balbine Noah, tenu des propos diffamatoires à l’encontre du MRC et de certains de ses responsables. Il s’agit des propos portant atteinte à la dignité de l’ancien président Maurice Kamto, de ceux traitant Olivier Bibou Nissack de « déséquilibré » et de ceux alléguant que le Pr Alain Fogue était « terroriste » et « tribaliste ». Qu’il a « lancé une cabale contre Cabral ». Le parti politique a alors exigé que Times TV et les médias cesse d’offrir des plateaux aux exclus ; que le CNC et la justice fassent la lumière sur les propos tenus sur Times TV, que « l’on cesse de confondre liberté d’expression et liberté de diffamer ». Le même jour, la télévision de Joël Kouemo a présenté ses excuses au MRC. Dans une communication, la chaîne de télévision dit prendre au sérieux les préoccupations exprimées par le parti politique. « Times TV présente ses regrets aux responsables du MRC visés par des propos outrageants et des attaques personnelles au cours de certaines de ses émissions ». La chaîne reconnait dans le même document des manquements lors de ces émissions décriées par la formation politique. Il s’agit en l’occurrence des manquements d’abord sur l’encadrement des intervenants. A ce sujet, « la confrontation des opinions, même vive, doit préserver la dignité des personnes et s’appuyer sur des arguments et des faits vérifiables », regrette la chaine. Ensuite sur la présentation de ces derniers, celle de Willy Mengue en particulier. Présenté sur l’affiche comme « homme politique MRC », il s’est réclamé du « MRC originel » au cours de l’émission. Une présentation initiale ambiguë, reconnait la chaîne. Ainsi, la chaîne de télévision s’engage à renforcer la vigilance dans la conduite des débats et réaffirme l’ouverture de ses portes aux Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun. items.title: Nasarawa vows to strengthen VAPP law implementation
items.description: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The Nasarawa State Government has reiterated its commitment to tackling gender-based violence through the implementation of the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Law, enacted in the state in January 2021. The Commissioner for Women Affairs and Social Development, Rebecca Adamu Kwaji, gave the assurance on Wednesday at a two-day workshop on bridging gaps in the implementation of the VAPP Law through policy dialogue, capacity building, institutional compliance and accountability among duty-bearers. The workshop, held at Awa Diamond Hotel, Lafia, was organised with the support of CLEEN Foundation. Kwaji said the state government had demonstrated the political will to address gender-based violence by incorporating the VAPP Law into the state’s legal framework. She expressed optimism that stronger implementation of the law would help reduce cases of gender-based violence. “With this programme in place, I want to say it will bring about a reduction in gender-based violence,” she said. The commissioner said the ministry, through its Social Welfare Department, had been handling cases of gender-based violence, with alleged perpetrators prosecuted and survivors provided with care and support. She added that the ministry had established a shelter where survivors could receive assistance and remain safe until they recovered and could be separated from their abusers. Kwaji commended CLEEN Foundation for selecting Nasarawa as one of its focal states for efforts to strengthen stakeholders’ capacity to implement the law, improve public awareness and increase its visibility among residents. She expressed hope that the workshop would encourage stronger enforcement of the law and help stakeholders identify practical ways to address implementation challenges. “CLEEN Foundation has really come to take a very good position in our midst to help us put this law to be appreciated, because this Violence Against Persons law has been in place, but I don’t see it much executed, as not so much emphasis [has been] placed on it,” she said. “I believe that after this programme, this law will be very much recognised, and something new will be added to it,” she added. Implementation gaps Earlier, the Executive Director of CLEEN Foundation, Peter Maduoma, said discussions on the VAPP Law centred on human rights, access to justice, public safety, institutional accountability and the protection of vulnerable persons. Maduoma, who was represented by the foundation’s Senior Programme Officer, Bernard Ekobay, acknowledged the support of the Royal Norwegian Embassy, saying its partnership had created opportunities for policy engagement, institutional strengthening and practical action towards more responsive and accountable justice and security institutions in Nigeria. He described the VAPP Law as an important legal framework for preventing violence, protecting survivors and holding perpetrators accountable. However, he said the existence of a law, regardless of how progressive its provisions might be, did not automatically guarantee justice for those who needed its protection. “The real test of the law is not simply whether it has been enacted, but whether a person experiencing domestic violence can safely seek help and receive a timely response; whether a survivor of sexual violence can report an incident without intimidation, stigma, or victim-blaming; whether a child exposed to abuse can access appropriate protection; and whether the institutions responsible for investigation, prosecution, adjudication, rehabilitation, and support can work together effectively,” he said. Maduoma identified limited public awareness of legal protections and reporting channels, poor coordination among relevant institutions, and weak or inconsistent investigation and prosecution as some of the challenges that could undermine implementation. He also listed inadequate survivor support services, resource and capacity constraints, and social pressures that discourage reporting or promote informal settlements in cases requiring legal accountability and survivor protection. He said stakeholders needed to establish the specific challenges affecting Nasarawa, identify weaknesses in institutional processes, assess existing successes and determine feasible reforms. “We need to understand which challenges are most pronounced in Nasarawa State, where institutional processes break down, what is already working, and which reforms are feasible within existing structures,” he said. He urged participants to engage constructively and work towards translating the law’s provisions into meaningful protection for residents. VAPP Law provides for compensation Also speaking, the Chairperson of the International Federation of Women Lawyers (FIDA), Nasarawa State chapter, Halima Hudu Abubakar, said the workshop could help improve the prosecution of offenders and strengthen the state’s response to gender-based violence. Abubakar said the Penal Code previously used in the state did not adequately address all forms of abuse, particularly physical, economic, sexual and emotional violence. She said the VAPP Law introduced provisions that could enable victims to seek compensation, in addition to the prosecution of offenders. “Before the coming of the VAPP Law, no law talked about compensating the victim. Only the offenders used to be prosecuted. Some of them don’t even know that they are supposed to go to court to seek for their rights,” she said. She argued that compensation could help victims obtain redress and reinforce accountability, while potentially discouraging repeat offences. Abubakar added that the full implementation of the law would help curb gender-based violence in Nasarawa State. items.title: Ebola: 5 things to know about Bundibugyo Strain as Nigeria confirms first case
items.description: Nigeria has confirmed its first case of Ebola virus disease caused by the Bundibugyo strain, prompting renewed attention to the symptoms, transmission, treatment and prevention of the infection. The World Health Organization (WHO) confirmed on October 20, 2026, that the patient was a woman with a recent travel history to Uganda. She was receiving medical care in isolation in Abuja, while 44 contacts had been identified and were being monitored. Here are five things to know about the Bundibugyo Ebola strain. 1. Bundibugyo is a distinct Ebola virus species Bundibugyo strain is one of the viruses known to cause Ebola virus disease in humans. It was first identified during an outbreak in Bundibugyo District, Uganda, in 2007. It is different from the Zaire ebolavirus species, which has caused several major Ebola outbreaks. The distinction matters because vaccines and treatments developed for one species may not protect against or treat another. 2. Symptoms include fever, weakness and diarrhoea Bundibugyo Ebola can cause symptoms that initially resemble those of other infections. Common symptoms include: Fever Severe weakness and fatigue Headache and muscle pain Abdominal pain Vomiting and diarrhoea In severe cases, patients may experience bleeding and complications affecting vital organs. However, bleeding does not occur in every case. Anyone experiencing compatible symptoms after possible exposure should seek prompt medical attention and tell healthcare workers about their travel history or contact with a suspected case. 3. The virus spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids Bundibugyo Ebola can spread through direct contact with the blood and other bodily fluids of an infected person who is ill. Transmission can also occur through contaminated objects and contact with infected animals. The virus can enter the body through broken skin or the eyes, nose and mouth. Healthcare workers and family members caring for infected people may be at risk if appropriate infection-prevention measures are not followed. The incubation period for Ebola generally ranges from two to 21 days, meaning symptoms may take up to three weeks to appear after infection. 4. There is no licensed vaccine or specifically approved treatment for the strain According to the WHO, there are currently no licensed vaccines or specifically approved therapeutics for preventing or treating Bundibugyo virus disease. This differs from Ebola disease caused by the Zaire ebolavirus species, for which licensed vaccines and treatments are available. However, supportive medical care remains important. It may include intravenous fluids, correction of electrolyte imbalances, oxygen support, nutritional support and treatment of complications. The WHO has identified candidate vaccines and treatments for evaluation in clinical trials, including the remdesivir antiviral and experimental monoclonal antibodies. These candidates should not be confused with established, specifically approved treatments for Bundibugyo Ebola. 5. Early detection and preventive measures are essential Preventing further transmission depends on identifying suspected cases quickly, isolating infected patients, tracing their contacts and monitoring exposed people for symptoms. Nigerians can reduce their risk by washing their hands regularly, avoiding contact with the blood and bodily fluids of suspected cases, and not handling sick or dead wild animals. Anyone who becomes unwell after possible exposure should seek medical attention promptly and provide accurate information about recent travel and contact with infected people. The NCDC and WHO remain key sources of official updates on the outbreak, case numbers and public health guidance. items.title: Flood submerges 18 Nasarawa communities, kills two
items.description: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The Nasarawa State Government has urged residents of flood-prone communities to heed warnings to relocate from low-lying areas to higher ground to avoid being swept away by recurring floods. The Commissioner for Information, Culture and Tourism, Dr Nawani Aboki, made the appeal on Monday while briefing journalists on the recent flooding that submerged 18 communities in a development area of Doma Local Government Area of the state. Aboki said two people had died in the disaster, while several residents had been displaced and buildings and farmlands destroyed. He said Governor Abdullahi Sule had directed the Director-General of the Nasarawa State Emergency Management Agency (NASEMA) to visit the affected communities to assess the extent of the damage and identify the necessary interventions. The commissioner said the government was expected to take concrete action following the assessment. “We are hoping that anytime this week, concrete actions will be taken by the government. Yesterday, when I was returning, I was there with the chairman of the local government to sympathise with the people and also condole with them,” he said. Describing the incident as massive flooding, Aboki expressed hope that the water would recede to allow residents to resume their normal activities. “It is not just normal flooding, but massive flooding that took place. We are hoping that the flooding will end and the waters will dry up so that people can resume their normal activities,” he said. He, however, warned residents against returning to their homes until the floodwaters had receded, citing concerns about the possibility of additional water flowing from the Lagdo Dam in Cameroon. “But we have asked them not to go back yet. Let them wait until we see the water actually receding back to the River Benue again. We are not sure if more water will be coming in from the Lagdo Dam in Cameroon. It will even be worse than it is currently,” he added. Aboki also reiterated the government’s commitment to providing support and relief supplies to the affected communities to prevent possible disease outbreaks. He explained that several smaller communities were clustered around larger settlements in the affected areas, increasing the pressure on host communities as displaced residents sought shelter. The commissioner cited Agyma, where more than eight communities were reportedly staying within the larger settlement, and Rukubi and Akpanaja, where several communities were also clustered. The government said it would continue to assess the situation and determine the necessary interventions as residents await the recession of the floodwaters. items.title: HCPAN to FG, States: Expand health insurance, review providers’ tarriffs
items.description: … Says 70% of healthcare spending comes from patients’ pockets … Only 10–13% of Nigerians covered by insurance … Seeks flexible premiums, prompt claims settlement By Chioma Obinna The HealthCare Providers Association of Nigeria (HCPAN), Lagos Branch, has called on the Federal and state governments to expand health insurance coverage, review tariffs paid to healthcare providers and ensure prompt settlement of claims, warning that low insurance penetration continues to expose millions of Nigerians to crippling medical expenses. The association said only about 10 to 13 per cent of Nigerians were covered by health insurance, while out-of-pocket payments accounted for approximately 70 per cent of healthcare expenditure, leaving many households financially vulnerable whenever illness occurs. HCPAN also called for flexible premium arrangements and community-based insurance schemes to bring market traders, artisans, transport workers, micro-entrepreneurs and other informal-sector workers into the health insurance system. The association made the call at its Scientific Conference and Annual General Meeting, AGM, held in Lagos, with the theme, “Expanding Health Insurance Coverage in Nigeria: Improving Community-Based Insurance Schemes in the Informal Sector.” Speaking at the event, the Chairman of HCPAN Lagos Branch, Pharmacist Biola Paul-Ozieh, said the country’s high dependence on direct payments for healthcare remained a major obstacle to achieving universal health coverage, despite the mandatory health insurance provisions of the National Health Insurance Authority, NHIA, Act, 2022. “Currently, it is reported that about 10 to 13 per cent of the Nigerian population is covered by health insurance. The out-of-pocket expenditure is still huge at roughly 70 per cent despite the mandatory clause in the NHIA Act 2022,” she said. Paul-Ozieh added that coverage of vulnerable groups stood at about 3.8 million, while participation among informal-sector workers remained limited, with enrolment concentrated mainly in Lagos and Abuja. She identified delayed claims payments, tariffs that failed to reflect prevailing economic realities, negative attitudes among some enrollees and the exclusion of certain healthcare professionals from insurance programmes as challenges undermining providers’ participation. “The other concern we have as providers is the various challenges faced by varied professionals in not being included in the provision of health services in the health insurance programme,” she said. The HCPAN chairman said sustainable community-based insurance schemes would require stronger collaboration between government and private healthcare providers, alongside policies that addressed the financial realities of informal-sector workers. Informal sector holds key to wider coverage The Chief Executive Officer of DrugStoc Limited, Dr Chibuzo Opara, who delivered the keynote address through his representative, Dr Damilare Ojo, said expanding enrolment alone would not guarantee universal health coverage unless insurance schemes enabled beneficiaries to obtain the treatment and medicines they needed. “What does it mean to have health insurance if, when illness occurs, the person cannot access the care needed?” he asked. Opara said insurance coverage remained concentrated in the formal sector, leaving traders, artisans, transport workers and small-business owners inadequately protected against healthcare costs. He explained that irregular incomes made fixed insurance contributions difficult for many informal-sector workers, stressing that schemes must be designed around their economic circumstances. “We cannot close this gap by simply increasing enrolment in existing schemes. If we genuinely want to achieve universal health coverage, we must develop insurance models that address the needs of the people we intend to cover,” he said. He advocated flexible contributions, appropriate benefit packages and group enrolment through trusted associations to encourage participation. Opara also called for community pharmacies to be integrated into insurance networks, describing them as accessible points where residents could obtain initial healthcare advice and medicines. He urged stakeholders to assess the effectiveness of insurance schemes through measurable outcomes, including access to medicines, service utilisation, referral outcomes, claims processing times, policy renewals and reductions in out-of-pocket expenditure. Lagos expands grassroots enrolment Meanwhile, the Lagos State Government has reaffirmed its commitment to expanding health insurance through affordable premiums, grassroots enrolment and the integration of community pharmacies and diagnostic centres into the healthcare network. The state Commissioner for Health, Professor Akin Abayomi, represented by the Deputy Director of the Research Unit at the Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr Tolu Babatope, said the informal sector accounted for a significant proportion of Lagos residents who often struggled to pay for medical treatment. He said the Lagos State Health Management Agency, LASHMA, was expanding affordable premium options and grassroots enrolment initiatives in line with the state’s policy on mandatory health insurance. Abayomi described community pharmacies as important entry points into the healthcare system, noting that their integration into insurance schemes could bring services closer to residents and strengthen access to treatment. “Community pharmacies, therefore, are no longer merely places where medicines are dispensed. They can serve as important points of contact for healthcare services and entry points into the health insurance network,” he said. He disclosed that the state was also working to strengthen links between pharmacies, hospitals and diagnostic centres, while addressing concerns about tariffs, delayed claims payments and inadequate digital infrastructure. Delivering the sub-theme, the Lagos Zonal Coordinator of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA), Pharmacist Femi Adeoye, who was represented by the State Coordinator, NHIA, Yaba Office, Pharmacist Chinenye Nwaohiri, highlighted opportunities for different healthcare professionals to participate in expanding health insurance. Adeoye said the NHIA operated programmes covering formal-sector workers, informal groups, private-sector participants and state health insurance schemes, with health maintenance organisations also supporting service delivery. He explained that initiatives such as the Basic Health Care Provision Fund and the Vulnerable Group Fund were designed to improve access to healthcare for people who might otherwise struggle to afford treatment. He called for fair tariff reviews that reflected the cost of providing services and urged healthcare professionals to take advantage of opportunities within the insurance system. “Fair tariff reviews and timely payment for services are essential to encouraging healthcare providers to participate in health insurance schemes and ensuring sustainable service delivery.” He stressed that public confidence depended on enrollees receiving timely and appropriate care, adding that reliable service delivery was essential to sustaining participation in insurance schemes. In his goodwill message, the National President of HCPAN, Dr Austin Aipoh, called for stronger collaboration among stakeholders and flexible payment arrangements to make health insurance more accessible to informal-sector workers. Aipoh said community-based approaches could help reach people whose incomes were irregular and who might not be able to afford conventional insurance contributions. He also urged policymakers to create an enabling environment for healthcare providers, stressing that insurance schemes must be structured to support both patients and the professionals responsible for delivering care.
