items.title: Landmark biodiversity fund collapses with just $7,085 raised
items.description: PARIS: Conceived at the 2024 Biodiversity COP, the Cali Fund was meant to raise billions of dollars for nature protection — but has so far only collected $7,085. It is a sluggish start for a fund intended as a showcase for innovative financing that charges companies profiting from the use of genetic data derived from nature. The trickle of money highlights the difficulties involved in mobilising money for biodiversity. As a crucial UN biodiversity summit in Armenia running until Oct 30 discusses its future, here’s a rundown on how the fund works and reasons for its lacklustre start: How does the fund work? Adopted at COP16 in Cali, Colombia, at the end of 2024, the fund began operating in February 2025. It proposes the payment of one percent of the annual profits of pharmaceutical, cosmetics, biotechnology companies or firms specialising in animal and plant breeding, or 0.1pc of their turnover. In a preparatory document, its designers mentioned the possibility of recovering one billion dollars a year in light of the revenues of the sectors concerned. However, so far only three companies have contributed: the British firms TierraViva AI ($1,000) and Prozomix ($5,000), and the Belgian company E-BIOM ($1,085). Two others have pledged an additional $3,571. What is its justification? Digital sequence information (DSI) — data derived from genetic resources such as plants, animals, fungi, viruses and micro-organisms — is freely accessible in digital databases. Companies draw on this biological heritage to turn it into economic value by developing a medicine, a cream, improving an agricultural plant and so on. The Cali Fund is based on the idea that those who benefit from this information, directly or indirectly, should in return contribute to the protection of biodiversity and to the local communities preserving it. The fund is not legally binding but it does invite states to adopt administrative, policy or legislative measures to encourage companies to do so. Why are companies reluctant? The main difficulty is that “mechanism still relies very heavily on incentives and voluntary contributions,” according to Juliette Landry from the sustainable development think tank IDDRI based in Paris. “As long as these incentives are not strong enough and consistent across countries, a company may well ask why it should contribute when its competitors are not doing so.” Pakhi Das, public policy adviser at the NGO Plant-for-the-Planet, said there were no countries currently with legislation incentivising contributions to the fund, nor are there any where such legislation is under discussion. Beyond the challenge of drawing enough resources into it, another lies in the actual use of the money collected. “The main hurdle that companies seem to be raising is ensuring there are safeguards in place for how their funding will be used,” said Vishaish Uppal, a director at WWF-India. Companies also want to be sure that the Cali Fund’s internationally accepted certificates — documenting receipt of payment for use of genetic resources — are also accepted nationally, to avoid paying twice. What does the pharmaceutical industry say? “The level of participation in the Cali Fund reflects ongoing questions about the design and implementation of the mechanism, rather than a lack of commitment to biodiversity,” said Guilherme Cintra, the director of innovation policy at the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Pakistan warns India against attempt to alter strategic balance
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Adviser to the National Command Authority retired Lt Gen Khalid Kidwai on Tuesday warned that Pakistan could review its deployment options to restore strategic balance in South Asia, saying India was moving towards a more prepared, potentially first-use capable nuclear posture. “Pakistan never has and never will accept strategic imbalances to be induced in South Asia,” Mr Kidwai said at the second Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference, hosted by the Strategic Vision Institute, an Islamabad based think tank specialising in strategic issues. “Pakistan will review and reconsider all options for appropriate deployments in order to restore the strategic balance and strategic stability while retaining the policy of strategic ambiguity,” he added. Mr Kidwai and retired Lt Gen Sarfraz Sattar, both former heads of the Strategic Plans Division and advisers to the NCA, said India’s reported deployment of nuclear weapons aboard a submarine, alongside missile modernisation and recent military confrontations, raised the risk of escalation between the two neighbouring arch rivals. NCA adviser reminds India of Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence policy Nuclear warheads Citing the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s SIPRI Yearbook 2026 and other publicly available information, they pointed to reports that India had deployed around 12 nuclear warheads on a submarine for deterrence patrols. They also cited missile canisterisation and wider nuclear and conventional modernisation as developments that cast doubt on India’s declared No-First-Use policy. Mr Kidwai said the reported deployment suggested India had mated nuclear warheads with submarine launched ballistic missiles and begun sea based deterrence patrols. “I do not see any reason as to why an SIPRI report might be inaccurate or speculative,” he said. “This irresponsible escalatory transition towards creating asymmetry in nuclear posture will have profound destabilising effects on South Asian strategic stability,” he added. Mr Kidwai said India’s ability to maintain a continuous at sea deterrent further undermined the credibility of its No-First-Use policy and pointed to a more offensive nuclear posture. “The operational reality that emerges is that India can undertake a first strike against Pakistan at zero notice,” he said. Advance notification He also questioned the absence of advance notification for Indian submarine launched ballistic missile tests, warning that such developments could heighten the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. Referring to the February 2019 confrontation, he said India had reportedly deployed its Arihant nuclear submarine in the Indian Ocean after carrying out air strikes near Balakot in Pakistan, presumably with nuclear weapons aboard. He described the latest reported deployment as part of India’s wider effort to operationalise mated nuclear weapons on submarines. “Pakistan reserves the right to undertake all appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and preserve strategic balance in the region under all circumstances,” Mr Kidwai said. He urged India to understand the implications of Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence policy. “India in fact will be well advised to read and re-read Pakistan’s policy of Full Spectrum Deterrence and seriously absorb its wide ranging implications for strategic deterrence, strategic stability, and for India’s security,” he said. Mr Sattar said the May 2025 conflict between the nuclear-armed neighbours showed how quickly conventional hostilities could escalate. The ceasefire came after both sides used cruise and ballistic missiles and India deployed strategic naval assets, he said. He drew parallels with the 2019 confrontation, when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi referred to the deployment of nuclear submarines for deterrence patrols and the positioning of BrahMos missiles along Pakistan’s border. The May 2025 fighting was more intense, involving kamikaze drones, supersonic BrahMos missiles capable of carrying conventional or nuclear warheads, and cyber and electronic warfare, he said. “It is now clear that the 2025 conflict was much more lethal in comparison to the 2019 conflict,” Mr Sattar said, warning that the fighting risked spiralling towards nuclear escalation through accident or miscalculation. He cited India’s canisterisation of land and sea based missiles, pursuit of multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle (MIRV) capabilities, short-range tactical missiles, ballistic missile defences, hypersonic weapons and autonomous platforms as further sources of concern. Combined with India’s Cold Start doctrine, wider military modernisation and the absence of a bilateral arms control mechanism, these developments raised doubts about its No-First-Use declaration and traditionally recessed deterrence posture, he said. “Rather, as I said, it signals a shift towards more first use capable posture,” Mr Sattar said. “The future strategic stability in South Asia is placed on a perilous and worrisome course with heightened risk of misunderstanding and miscalculation, potentially leading to unintended or accidental escalation to the nuclear level,” he added. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: BYD to rely on imports initially, Hubco says
items.description: KARACHI: Hub Power Company (Hubco) has said that BYD vehicle production will initially rely entirely on imported raw materials and components, with localisation increasing gradually over time. The long-term objective is to localise up to 80 per cent of the vehicle, which should improve cost competitiveness and reduce reliance on imports, Hubco management said during a corporate briefing held on October 20, 2026. Topline Securities said the BYD plant is expected to commence operations within the next 4-5 weeks, by mid-December. The management is targeting an initial sales run rate of approximately 1,000-1,500 BYD vehicles per month as production ramps up. BYD plans to introduce additional models through a phased approach, focusing on segments that can generate meaningful sales volumes, the brokerage house said. According to Topline Securities, Lucky Cement told analysts on Tuesday that competition in the EV segment remains intense, particularly from Chinese completely built-up (CBU) vehicles. The company aims to begin local production of EV models by the first quarter of calendar year 2027, with volumes and model offerings expected to increase gradually in subsequent quarters. items.title: Judicial Commission of Pakistan’s transfer-only policy for IHC judges challenged
items.description: ISLAMABAD: A writ petition filed in the Islamabad High Court has challenged the Judicial Commission of Pakistan’s (JCP) April 28 decision that vacancies arising from the transfer of a judge “shall be filled through transfer only”, arguing that the three vacant judges’ seats in the IHC should be filled through fresh appointments under the Constitution rather than further transfers. The petition, filed by Advocate Supreme Court Syed Nayyab Hassan Gardezi against the Federation of Pakistan, JCP, president and prime minister, contends that the impugned decision has no constitutional foundation and conflicts with Article 175A(8), which requires the commission to nominate one person “for each vacancy” of a high court judge. It argues that the Constitution recognises no category of high court vacancy exempt from this requirement and that the commission cannot create one through a resolution. The petition contends that the JCP decision was taken in disregard of the procedure prescribed by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (Appointment of Judges) Rules 2024. It points out that Rule 11(2) requires the secretary to notify all members at least 14 days before a scheduled meeting, providing the agenda and supporting materials. According to the petition, the impugned decision was reportedly introduced during the proceedings rather than being included in the circulated agenda. It further states that the JCP Rules, as notified, contain no provision for their amendment, while the only provision allowing the commission to remove difficulties — Rule 15 — requires the votes of at least two-thirds of its total membership. The impugned decision, however, records only a “majority of its total membership”. The petition also questions the composition of the JCP when the decision was taken. It argues that the impugned decision governs future appointments to the IHC, yet it was taken at meetings convened to consider transfers, at which the commission sat under the first proviso to Article 200(1), with the chief justices of the high courts concerned in each transfer. By contrast, the Constitution prescribes a distinct composition for the appointment of IHC judges under Article 175A(6). Besides the IHC chief justice, it includes the head of IHC’s constitutional benches, an advocate nominated by the Islamabad Bar Council and a federal minister nominated by the prime minister. The petitioner submits that procedural and compositional defects reinforce the need for the IHC’s three vacancies, created by the transfers notified on April 29, 2026, to be filled through the constitutional process of fresh appointments. For this purpose, nominations should be invited from members of the commission under Article 175A(23) and Rule 9(1) of the JCP Rules, rather than through a transfer-only route. The petition also challenges the decision on grounds of discrimination, retrospectivity and an unlawful fetter on discretion. It notes that in July 2026, the JCP filled vacancies in the Lahore High Court, Sindh High Court and Baloc­histan High Court through initial appointments, while the IHC’s vacancies have been reserved for transfers. It emphasises that the IHC is currently functioning with a chief justice and nine judges against a sanctioned strength of a chief justice and 12 judges, and that the three vacancies have remained unfilled for more than five months. Along with the writ petition, the petitioner has filed an application for interim relief, seeking to restrain the respondents from recommending, advising or notifying the transfer of any judge to the IHC against the three vacancies while the petition remains pending. The petition seeks a declaration that the JCP’s decision is ultra vires Articles 4, 25, 175A and 193 of the Constitution and the JCP Rules, and is of no legal effect. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Makkah alliance binds partners to decade-long pact
items.description: • Turkiye seeks parliamentary nod for defence agreement; officials say Ankara’s support may be limited to provision of weapons, equipment and intelligence sharing • Pakistan has already ratified treaty; only PM and cabinet’s nod required under Article 90 • Egypt’s parliament to vote on support for Riyadh on Oct 26 • Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar and Indonesia expected to sign defence cooperation agreement in Doha today ANKARA: Turkiye has submitted the Makkah defence pact to parliament for ratification, moving Nato’s second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it continues to face Houthi attacks. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The provision, similar to Nato’s Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attacks. All three members have agreed to use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, as per the text seen by Reuters. The agreement will enter into force upon the deposit of the ratification documents with the secretariat in Riyadh, and will remain valid indefinitely. The parties may not withdraw from the agreement for the first 10 years. While Pakistan has made it clear that ‘collective deterrence measures’ under the trilateral defence agreement are “already in play”, Ankara still requires formal parliamentary ratification for the agreement. According to official sources, Pakistan follows an executive-led treaty-making system, where the federal government’s ratification is enough for subjects in the federal legislative list. According to Article 90 of the Constitution, “the executive authority of the Federation shall be exercised in the name of the President by the Federal Government, consisting of the Prime Minister and the Federal Ministers, which shall act through the Prime Minister, who shall be the chief executive of the Federation.” However, under Tur­kiye’s constitution, separate permission from parliament is required to deploy troops abroad, regardless of any international agreement. According to the Reuters news agency, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtu­lmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, is expected to refer the agreement to parliament’s foreign affairs commission upon his ret­urn, which could debate the agreement as early as Friday. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s communications director, Burha­nettin Dur­an, said that Turk­iye’s re­cent step marked an important mile­stone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations. “This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to stre­ngthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region,” Duran said in a post on X. A Turkish official, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity, said Turkiye’s own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far. Asked how Turkiye could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Makkah Agree­ment was not an “offensive agreement,” adding that Turkiye would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory. Although not part of the Makkah alliance, Egypt’s parliament is also expe­cted to vote on authorising pote­ntial military support for Saudi Arabia on Oct 26. Ahead of its submission for parliamentary appr­oval, the contents of the agreement were published in full for the first time by Turkish state broadcaster, TRT Haber. Turkiye, which has a rob­ust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh’s military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against “all means of terrorism,” including at the operational level. Defence deal Meanwhile, TRT World also reported that Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia are expected to sign a defence industry cooperation memorandum today (Wednesday). The signing will be held in Qatar, which is also expected to announce plans to establish a local defence production hub, the Gulf state’s Minister of State for Defence Affairs Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani told the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday. Turkish Defence Mini­ster Yasar Guler will travel to Doha for the signing. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who was also in Doha for the security for­um , is expected to represent Pakistan at the signing. Earlier, Mr Naqvi met with his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, who also commands Qatar’s Internal Security Force (Lekhwiya). The two discussed the current regional situation and matters concerning regional peace and stability, the state-run APP news agency reported. During their meeting, the two men agreed to expand the security partnership between Pakistan and Qatar. They also held detailed discussions on expanding cooperation in areas related to internal security. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: CDF Munir-Pezeshkian meeting raises peace hopes
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Iranian leaders have told Pakistan that the United States must take the first steps to rebuild trust, and that the acceptance of Tehran’s seven-point proposal could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations. The message was conveyed during Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir’s visit on Tuesday, where he met with President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Bagher Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, a representative of Iran’s supreme leader and secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also accompanied the army chief. As diplomatic efforts intensified to prevent a resumption of hostilities, Field Marshal Munir’s visit is being viewed as a move to quell escalating regional tensions. Tehran says acceptance of its 7-point proposal can be starting point for renewed talks with US The visit came a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks with Iranian leaders on the conflict and efforts to restore regional stability. The visit was aimed at conveying messages and exploring whether the Islamabad understanding could still provide a basis for negotiations, but no breakthrough or formal agreement was announced after Tuesday’s meetings. The discussions also touched on bilateral relations, including a recent disruption in commercial trade across the Pakistan-Iran border. Iranian officials also raised concerns over the closure, while Field Marshal Munir told them that the border closure was temporary and due to technical reasons and that the crossings had reopened on Tuesday. Importantly, Iranian officials reportedly shared with the field marshal their response to a US proposal, reiterating that Tehran would not make concessions under pressure and that Washington must meet its conditions before trust could be restored. While there was no official word from Pakistan’s Foreign Office or Inter-Services Public Relations, Iranian media described the response as “clear, serious, and explicit”. An Iranian source said the visiting Pakistani army chief was told that “Iran has nothing new to say to the Americans” and it was for them to return to Islamabad Memorandum. Although not many details about President Pezeshkian’s meeting were released to media, in a post that was unrelated to his meeting with Field Marshal Munir, the president said that Iranians may endure hardship, but they will not surrender their land. Speaker Ghalibaf told Field Marshal Munir that the US could not regain Iran’s trust without fulfilling the seven conditions Tehran had presented during meetings in New York. He said Washington’s past actions, including what Iran considers a violation of the Islamabad understanding, had only deepened its distrust of the US administration. “Threats and military manoeuvres cannot influence the strategic decisions of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Mr Ghalibaf said, according to an Iranian account of the meeting, adding that it was now up to Washington to take the necessary steps to extricate itself from the conflict. Mr Rezaei, meanwhile, said Iran would not surrender its enriched nuclear material, describing it as a national asset intended for domestic use. He said Iranian officials were united in their view that negotiations could not proceed without steps by Washington to meet Tehran’s conditions. The inflexible Iranian response has thrown a challenge for Pakistan, which has sought to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran after an earlier diplomatic breakthrough failed to produce a lasting settlement. Islamabad brokered a ceasefire in April and hosted direct talks that led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June. The agreement outlined steps towards easing the conflict, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic and nuclear issues, but the process subsequently stalled after disagreements. Despite the breakdown of the peace process, Pakistan has continued to offer its good offices to both sides for preventing another round of fighting. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: IMF urges Pakistan to move beyond fiscal targets
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has called for Pakistan’s fiscal policy to go beyond achieving primary balance targets and protecting debt sustainability by reinforcing policy credibility, fostering economic recovery and creating space for public investment and social spending to support stronger long-term growth. Speaking at a workshop on “Reforms for a Modern and Growth-Friendly Tax System in Pakistan”, IMF Middle East and Central Asia Department Director Jihad Azour said tax refo­rm was critical to Pak­is­tan’s economic growth agenda and rema­ined central to the objectives of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF). The workshop was organised by the Ministry of Finance and Revenue in collaboration with the IMF. Finance Minister Muha­mmad Aurangzeb also spoke at the workshop, highlighting achiev­ements over the past two years. Mr Azour said Pakistan had made important progress towards restoring macroeconomic stability, rebuilding confidence, strengthening external buffers and supporting a gradual economic recovery despite an era of shocks and uncertainty. Jihad Azour calls for broader, more predictable tax system The IMF official said Pakistan’s recent stabilisation gains had created an opportunity that needed to be strengthened through transformative reforms, with tax reform at the heart of the process. “A stronger, broader, fairer and more predictable tax system can support fiscal sustainability while reducing distortions that hold back investment, productivity, growth and formal job creation,” he remarked. He said broadening the tax base, strengthening revenue administration, reducing tax expenditures, protecting priority spending and improving public service provision were Pakistan’s priorities. He credited Pakistan for the progress made. However, he said the next milestone was to turn stabilisation into stronger and more durable growth by moving beyond cycles of adjustment towa­r­ds a more competitive, inv­e­s­tment-friendly and inclusive economy. Mr Azour said the IMF remained committed to supporting the authorities in building an economy capable of delivering hig­her productivity, led by a stronger private sector, and creating better opportunities for younger generations. He warned that the highly uncertain external environment had made these objectives more urgent. Fiscal policy, he said, must do more than achieve primary balance targets and protect debt sustainability. It must reinforce policy credibility, foster recovery and create space for public investment and social spending needed to support long-term growth and public welfare. Outlining four themes for discussion during the two-day workshop, Mr Azour identified credibility, growth, fairness and implementation as central to the reform process. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Draft auto policy sent to cabinet
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday approved the draft Auto Policy 2026-31, which aims to increase auto sector exports to $6 billion and boost local production, competitiveness and electric vehicle (EV) adoption. Although the Prime Minister’s Office did not issue an official statement, sources in the federal government shared the final draft, which was presented to the premier by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Adviser on Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar. The draft policy will be presented to the federal cabinet for in-principle approval, then it will need parliament’s nod. The policy aims to bring the auto sector to open competition by significantly reducing tariffs on completely built-up units (CBUs) and completely knocked-down (CKD) kits up to 15pc by 2030-31. PM ‘okays’ five-year roadmap; policy targets $6bn exports, tariff cuts by 2031; proposes 1pc sales tax on EVs Under the proposed draft, battery electric vehicles will be subject to a 1pc sales tax during 2026-31. The document proposes a 6pc sales tax on range-extended electric vehicles and a 9pc on plug-in hybrid vehicles. A 10pc federal excise duty has been proposed on electric vehicles valued more than $75,000. The policy also envisages lower tariffs on smaller electric vehicles priced below $15,000. To encourage EV adoption, the government has approved proposals to raise the financing limit from Rs3 million to Rs10m and extend the repayment period from three to five years, making smaller vehicles more affordable for low-income consumers. The government has set the total export target of $6.01bn during the five years of the policy, which includes combined exports of parts and vehicles amounting to $256.6m for 2026-27, $671.8m for 2027-28, $1.11bn for 2028-29, $1.17bn for 2029-30 and $2.19bn for 2030-31 the fifth year of the auto policy. The policy also proposes mandatory export targets for vehicle manufacturers, with incentives for companies that increase exports. Under the proposed incentive mechanism, manufacturers would receive compensation equivalent to 5pc of export value for boosting exports, along with an additional 10pc incentive on exports exceeding the previous year’s level. Companies that fail to meet their export targets would face penalties, and manufacturing certificates could be cancelled if targets remain unmet for two consecutive years. The policy also sets new targets to increase the use of locally manufactured auto parts. Companies failing to meet local production targets could lose their incentives. The government expects to collect more than Rs232bn through the Automotive Development Levy over five years. The proceeds would be used to finance export incentives and industrial development programmes, including funding for technology upgrades by auto parts manufacturers. The policy proposes levying the Automotive Development Levy on vehicles with engine capacities exceeding 1,000cc. To strengthen quality assurance and regulatory oversight, the government plans to establish the Pakistan Automotive Testing Institute. The policy also provides funding for research, certification, and third-party audits, as well as the adoption of international safety standards for locally manufactured and imported vehicles. Meanwhile, Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers (Paapam) Chairman Abdul Rehman Aizaz said the new policy, by lowering the import tariff on parts to 15pc, would phase out local parts manufacturers and benefit assemblers, warning that assemblers could eventually be phased out as imported cars take over.“This policy will make Pakistan an import destination country with no local industrial base in the auto sector,” he remarked. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: State of deceased’s eyes not proof of ‘unwitnessed’ death: SC
items.description: • Court dismisses petitions challenging double-murder convictions • Verdict explains that closing eyes of a corpse is ‘religious’ custom, not legal duty ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court ruled on Tuesday that the condition of a deceased person’s eyes at the time of death cannot conclusively establish the fact that the incident was not witnessed. The Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, 1984, does not impose a legal duty to close a deceased person’s eyes. Rather, the practice is customary and religious, observed Justice Salahuddin Panhwar while dismissing jail petitions filed by Azmat Ullah alias Motu and Muhammad Luqman alias Gona. The petitioners had challenged their convictions in a 2011 double-murder case, upheld by the Lahore High Court (LHC) on May 18, 2022. Justice Panhwar was part of a three-member bench, headed by Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar. The bench upheld the convictions under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code but maintained the high court’s decision to commute the death sentences to life imprisonment. In criminal trials, defence lawyers often argue that an incident was ‘unwitnessed’ if the post-mortem report records the deceased’s eyes as open, reasoning that close relatives would ordinarily close them after death. During the hearing, the petitioners’ counsel pointed to discrepancies in eyewitness statements and argued that the post-mortem and inquest reports, which recorded the eyes of both victims as open, indicated that the murders had not been witnessed. Article 129 versus rigid presumptions In a nine-page judgement, Justice Panhwar referred to Article 129 of the Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, which allows courts to presume facts they consider likely in the circumstances of a particular case. However, the judgement stressed that human behaviour could not be assessed in a vacuum or through rigid assumptions. Responses to trauma, terror and violent loss vary from person to person, making it unsafe to draw categorical conclusions from a single circumstance. It noted that relatives witnessing a gruesome incident may be overwhelmed by shock and trauma. Hoping their loved one might survive, they may focus on obtaining urgent medical assistance rather than performing customary rituals associated with death. Relatives and bystanders may also continue treating the victim as injured until a doctor or police official confirms death, which may not be immediately apparent at the scene. Other factors From a forensic perspective, the position of the eyelids is governed by physiological processes rather than the presence or absence of witnesses, the judgement explained. Following death, muscles initially become relaxed, allowing eyelids to remain open or partially open, a condition known as lagophthalmos. Handling or moving a body may also cause previously closed eyes to reopen, particularly before rigor mortis develops. As rigor mortis sets in, muscles become stiff and retain their prevailing position. The court also cited Locard’s Exchange Principle, which holds that every contact leaves a trace. Relatives, bystanders and rescue workers may avoid touching a body to prevent contamination or disturbance of blood-spatter patterns, trace evidence and DNA material before forensic experts arrive. It would therefore be unsafe to presume that every person knows how to handle a deceased body or feels obliged to close the eyes, the judgement said. Concluding that neither forensic literature nor the law recognises closed eyes as an indicator of a witnessed death, the court rejected the argument that open eyelids alone could establish that a crime was unwitnessed. The judgement further observed that minor discrepancies and natural variations in eyewitness accounts, arising from the passage of time and the rigours of cross-examination, do not undermine otherwise credible and consistent testimony. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Balochistan says Rs14bn spent to counter terrorism
items.description: • Insists 18 laws enacted, 17 institutions set up under security plans • Officials claim 60,000 operations conducted, 1,100 terrorists killed QUETTA: The Balochistan government has passed 18 laws, established 17 institutions and departments and spent more than Rs14 billion on counterterrorism measures under the National Action Plan, Counterterrorism Policy and Provincial Action Plan, senior provincial officials said on Tuesday. They also claimed that more than 60,000 counterterrorism operations had been conducted across Balochistan up to October, killing over 1,000 terrorists. The Counter-Terrorism Depart­ment alone had killed 250 terrorists and arrested another 250 suspects. They said 101 police personnel and around 200 members of other law enforcement agencies had lost their lives, while 551 civilians had been killed in terrorist violence. The figures were revealed during a joint press conference held by Provincial Home Minister Ziaullah Langove along with Chief Mini­ster’s Adviser on Media and Political Aff­a­irs Shahid Rind and Additional Chief Secretary Home Hamza Shafqaat. They said measures had also been taken to secure the Quetta-Rakhni, Quetta-Karachi and Quetta-Taftan highways and expressed confidence that the security situation would improve over the next three to four months. Mr Shafqaat said the provincial government had taken a series of measures over the past two years to implement the National Action Plan, Counter Terrorism Policy and Provincial Action Plan. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: BBC to close three TV, radio channels amid cost pressures
items.description: The BBC reported on Tuesday that it will close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation seeks to make 500 million pounds ($669 million) of savings over two years. Both services will become online-only, which means that they will continue to produce and host some content on iPlayer, without the need to fill a terrestrial TV schedule, according to the report. The BBC also announced that it will close Radio 4 Extra, which largely airs speech programs from the BBC's archive, including comedy, drama and documentaries. The decision was made in response to "immediate cost pressures," said BBC Director-General Matt Brittin, adding that "we all know that means tough choices." "Against the backdrop of significant financial challenges, we must focus our resources where they will have the greatest impact for audiences," said Director of BBC Scotland Hayley Valentine.

items.title: France to deploy military forces for next protests
items.description: France will deploy troops from its counterterrorism military forces to support police and gendarmes ahead of demonstrations expected on October 24, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend's violence. Speaking in the National Assembly, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the troops would mainly serve in static security roles, allowing police and gendarmes to focus on mobile law enforcement and respond more flexibly to potential violence. He told lawmakers that the security forces deployed on October 17 had been "not mobile enough." The government is also considering banning unauthorized demonstrations, as well as officially declared protests deemed at risk of spiraling out of control, Nunez said. "The deployment next Saturday will be massive," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities at the weekend. Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state's response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not cancelling planned police leave. France saw nationwide protests on October 17, with the government estimating that around 550,000 people took part, while organizers put the figure at 800,000. Some demonstrations were marred by violent clashes. According to official figures, at least 3,000 shops were looted nationwide. Some trade unions and student groups have set November 5 as the date for another nationwide protest. Meanwhile, some activists who took part in the October 17 demonstrations have called for further protests on October 24. Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 ​investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence. Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group. A night of relative ‌calm in France followed targeted curfews imposed in several areas on Monday affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localized curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said. (With input from agencies)

items.title: The Three Dates for Deciding Ukraine’s Future
items.description: O ver the next eight weeks , as winter envelopes Ukraine, Russia plans to use the frigid weather as a weapon. Its arms factories have already made enough missiles and drones to take down Ukraine’s electrical grid, as well as the heating systems that millions of people rely on to stay warm. Homes far from the front will become deadly for their inhabitants as temperatures fall. In that same time frame, three events taking place thousands of miles away could determine Ukraine’s future. The first is America’s Election Day, now two weeks away; leaders in Kyiv fear that if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress, President Trump may turn even further against them in those final weeks of full Republican control of Washington. The second is a proposed summit in mid-November in southern China, where Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to meet with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to plan how to end the war—without having a seat at the table for Ukraine. The third is the G20 summit at Trump’s Miami-area golf course, scheduled to take place in mid-December. The president has visions of standing between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as they sign a peace deal, even if he has to strong-arm Ukraine to do it, according to advisers. One Ukrainian official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss internal conversations, told us that it’s hard not to feel left out of decision making that will dictate the country’s future: “It looks like this is all happening without us.” The U.S. president, who used to brag that he could resolve the war in 24 hours, has tossed aside some sanctions on Russia and struck a deal with Putin to import diesel from Moscow, giving a boost to the Russian war machine. He and his allies have threatened Kyiv, demanding that Zelensky stop attacking Russian oil refineries or risk losing access to American intelligence, weaponry, and satellite communications that it uses to defend itself. The calendar is now Ukraine’s foe—and so, Ukrainians fear, is Donald Trump. T rump’s war in Iran has appeared to throttle Republicans’ chances in the midterms; the unending conflict, and the resulting surge in oil and gas prices, has eroded the GOP’s poll numbers and fueled Democrats’ hopes of taking both chambers of Congress. Stymied in his efforts to bring that war to a close, Trump recently shifted his focus to resolving the Ukraine conflict, in part to bring fuel prices down. But the way he’s chosen to try to do that has provided his fellow Republicans with a nasty October surprise . In a first for a U.S. president, Trump has sided with a traditional adversary, Russia, over a democracy that is not only fighting for its existence but also acting as a bulwark against a wider war. Trump’s diesel deal with Putin will have a negligible impact on American energy prices, but it’s a financial lifeline for Moscow. [ Read: Ukraine finds a new set of targets ] Trump has demanded an energy cease-fire—he even announced one earlier this month that had no basis in reality—yet has focused his ire entirely on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He blames those strikes for the rise in energy prices while ignoring the real culprit, Iran’s ability to defy the United States and close the Strait of Hormuz . He’s convinced himself, three people close to him have told us, that Ukraine’s attacks on the refineries are, in part, meant to undermine Republicans’ chances next month—and, by extension, Trump. The president has ignored Moscow’s attacks on Ukraine’s electrical grid, and yesterday, hours after a drone strike on a public park killed six people, including two children, he downplayed its strikes on Ukraine’s cities, declaring that Russia had not “been doing much.” An image of one of the dead children, a 1-year-old killed as she sat in her stroller, was broadcast around the globe. More pressure could be coming. Trump aides have threatened to withhold arms sales unless Kyiv stops targeting Russian diesel plants; this week, the administration delayed approving the transfer of missiles that Ukraine needs for its defense. Ukraine in the past week has said that it has not consistently received early warnings of attacks and no longer has full Starshield satellite access, which is impeding its ability to defend itself against Russia’s new fleet of jet-powered drones. ( The Wall Street Journal reported today that Starshield’s creator, Elon Musk, ordered the slowdown . The White House and Musk had previously denied involvement.) Some in Trump’s orbit have suggested that the United States go further and stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Trump’s deference to Putin has been a theme for a decade, yet this new round of kowtowing has handed Republicans another obstacle ahead of the elections. In a rare act of defiance, a handful in the party have denounced the president’s decisions, including his move to undercut a Russia-sanctions bill that he signed only a month ago in honor of its champion, the late Senator Lindsey Graham. The quick betrayal of Graham’s legacy was a blow for some of his Senate colleagues; GOP aides told us that Graham’s sudden July death cost Ukraine its most vocal champion in Trump’s inner circle, and that no one has stepped up to fill that void. Michael Froman, who worked in the Clinton and Obama administrations and is now president of the Council on Foreign Relations, told us that cutting off Kyiv from American weapons or intelligence might, in fact, prolong the war because it “would undermine Ukraine’s position at the negotiating table and make it less likely Russia would be willing to negotiate on any of the key outstanding issues.” Officials with both parties predict that the Democrats will capture the House next month; the Senate appears to be a true toss-up. Kyiv will be carefully watching the results. A Democratic win next month will, in the long run, likely help Kyiv, and some of the more hopeful members of Zelensky’s camp believe that Republican defeats could force Trump to focus more on domestic issues, resulting in him leaving Ukraine alone. But other observers on both sides of the Atlantic fear that the opposite could be true. A president without a friendly Congress tends to fall back more on foreign policy, where he needs little help from Capitol Hill. Either way, the new Congress won’t be seated until January 3, leaving Trump unchecked for two more months and perhaps motivated to wield power before his party moves into the minority. Another major national election would not be for two years—plenty of time for Trump to push Ukraine without fear of voters punishing Republicans. “He could get distracted at any time,” one outside Trump ally told us. “But right now, he’s furious at Ukraine, and he wants Zelensky gone.” T wo weeks after Election Day , Trump plans to board Air Force One bound for a series of summits in Asia. Earlier this month, Trump overruled White House aides who had counseled against him calling to wish Putin a happy birthday, warning that little good would come of it. In that conversation, Trump authorized the diesel deal, and Putin suggested something grander: a meeting of the world’s great powers to divide up the world. Or at least Ukraine. Putin proposed that he, Trump, and Xi hold a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China, in mid-November to discuss a variety of issues, including Ukraine. Trump told reporters yesterday that he is open to attending the meeting, which would be his first face-to-face encounter with Putin since their unproductive summit in Alaska last year. It is no surprise that Trump is drawn to the idea; his deference toward Putin is rivaled only by his regard for Xi, whom he hosted in lavish fashion at the White House last month. He has previously been intrigued by the idea of the three powers—China, Russia, the United States—dividing the globe into spheres of influence, although Moscow these days hardly wields the international clout of Washington or Beijing. [ Read: The deferential president ] The idea of two authoritarians and their admirer plotting to slice up sovereign nations alarmed much of the West. And how, Kyiv demanded, could Ukraine’s future be decided with no input from Ukraine? But some in Trump’s orbit have backed the idea, belittling Ukraine as a corrupt backwater with no autonomy. Putin has never viewed Ukraine as a legitimate country, and Trump has held a grudge against it since 2019, when he was impeached (for the first time) after pressuring Zelensky to dig up damaging information about Trump’s political rival Joe Biden. He and his Ukrainian counterpart had a shouting match at the White House early in Trump’s second term, causing the U.S. to briefly withhold intelligence. Since then, Zelensky has tried to flatter Trump to stay on his good side, but those niceties have vanished as the American president has demanded that Ukraine pick a new leader. Many of those in Trump’s orbit are unsympathetic to Ukraine’s plight and see the war not as a battle for the modern, rules-based world order—with its cardinal tenet prohibiting the seizure of land by force—but as an impediment to future business deals with Russia, some of which could enrich members of the president’s inner circle. Pushing Ukraine into taking a deal, even if that means it has to give up its claim on the Donbas, would open up avenues to dealmaking on Russia’s diesel, rare-earth minerals, and other resources. Zelensky has balked at any territorial concessions. “Our worry is that they are looking at this as a new Yalta Conference, to divide the world into spheres of influence,” another Ukrainian official told us. Trump’s ideal timeline for some sort of Russia-Ukraine peace agreement, as we reported last week, would be in December at the G20 summit. That bit of history, were it to occur, would take place at one of Trump’s own properties. In Trump’s first term, he pushed to host the 2020 G7 at his golf course in Doral, just outside of Miami. But Trump abandoned the idea amid bipartisan blowback over his plan to personally profit off the event. This time, there has been nary a Republican whimper of protest about Trump’s venue choice, but some have lodged complaints about the president’s other idea for the summit: to invite Putin. The Russian leader has yet to agree to show up, but if he does, it would be the first time he has attended a multilateral summit in a Western country since his invasion of Ukraine. It would allow him to take another step in shedding his status as an international pariah, though it is hard to imagine that European leaders are eager to talk with Putin. Zelensky, who has already committed to attending the G20, has made clear that he would be willing to sit down with Putin, no matter the venue, to work out an agreement to end the war. If Trump has his way over the next eight weeks, it might be not a negotiation, but a capitulation.

Journées régionales de l’agro-écologie des Tannounyan La Ire édition se tiendra les 22 et 23 octobre prochains à Banfora
items.description: La 1re édition des journées régionales de l’agroécologie des Tannounyan se tiendront, les 22 et 23 octobre prochains, à Banfora sur le thème « Agroécologie et résilience des communautés : stratégies et leviers d’action ». Les organisateurs ont annoncé les couleurs de l’évènement à travers une conférence de presse, le lundi 19 octobre 2026, dans la cité du Paysan noir. L’agroécologie va être à l’honneur, les 22 et 23 octobre, à Banfora. La ville va abriter en effet la Ire édition des journées régionales de l’agro-écologie des Tannounyan. L’information a été donnée par les organisateurs de l’évènement à travers une conférence de presse qu’ils ont animée dans l’après-midi du lundi 19 octobre 2026, dans la cité du Paysan noir. Le thème retenu est « Agroécologie et résilience des communautés : stratégies et leviers d’action ». Le principal conférencier, Larissa Kaboré, a indiqué que ces journées sont organisées par l’association Munyu des femmes, en collaboration avec la commune de Banfora, le Conseil national de l’agriculture biologique et le Cadre de concertation des acteurs de l’agroécologie et de l’agriculture biologique des Tannounyan. A l’écouter, l’évènement s’inscrit dans la continuité des journées nationales de l’agro-écologie dont la IIe édition s’est tenue en décembre 2025, et visent à prolonger cette dynamique à l’échelle régionale. Face aux défis auxquels font face les communautés tels que les changements climatiques et la dégradation des ressources naturelles, a-t-elle expliqué, l’agro-écologie offre des pistes d’actions pour renforcer la capacité des communautés à y faire face. Mais la transition agroécologique, a-t-elle poursuivi, outre les techniques agricoles, nécessite également une meilleure information des populations, la mobilisation des acteurs territoriaux et l’engagement de tous. Ces journées visent donc aux dires de Larissa Kaboré, à permettre aux acteurs des Tannounyan de s’approprier les enjeux liés à l’agro-écologie de partager leurs expériences et d’identifier des solutions adaptées à leurs réalités. Cela, avec pour objectif globale, de renforcer la résilience des communautés par la valorisation du potentiel agroécologique dans la région. Durant ce rendez-vous de deux jours, plusieurs communications et une mini-foire sont au menu. Des communications qui vont porter sur,entre autres thèmes, « Stratégie nationale de développement de l’agroécologie : acquis et perspectives », et « Agroécologie, recherche et innovation : leviers d’action pour la résilience des communautés ». Quant à la mini-foire, elle va permettre de mettre un point d’honneur sur les produits, les initiatives et les savoir-faire des acteurs régionaux. Quelles ambitions nourrit cet évènement à moyen et long terme ? A cette question de la presse, Mme Kaboré a confié qu’à long terme il vise la transition agroécologique, afin que les pratiques agroécologiques soient adoptées par les producteurs et par toute la communauté et que les produits agroécologiques le soient aussi par les consommateurs. Séance tenante, les conférenciers ont appelé les producteurs, les transformateurs, les organisations professionnelles, les organisations de la société civile et les services techniques, à se mobiliser pour la réussite de ces journées. Alpha Sékou BARRY alphasekoubarry@gmail.com

items.title: Translog Africa 2026 : faire des corridors de véritables axes de développement
items.description: La Ve édition du symposium international sur le Transport et la logistique (Translog Africa) se déroule, du 20 au 22 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou sur le thème : « Résilience et sécurisation des chaînes logistiques dans un environnement mondial en pleine mutation ». Les défis du transport et de la logistique appellent à des réponses concertées africaines et solidaires. C’est dans cette perspective que le Conseil burkinabè des chargeurs (CBC) organise à Ouagadougou, du 20 au 22 octobre 2026, la Ve édition du symposium international sur le Transport et la logistique (Translog Africa). L’évènement réunit plus de 150 experts de la chaine des transports et de la logistique de 15 pays étrangers, entre autres, le Mali, le Niger, le Cameroun, le Sénégal, le Benin, la Côte D’ivoire, le Togo, la Belgique et le Congo. L’ouverture de la rencontre est intervenue, le mardi 20 octobre 2026. Durant les trois jours, les échanges vont porter notamment sur la sécurisation des flux, la digitalisation, la performance des corridors, le financement des infrastructures et le rôle de la logistique dans l'industrialisation du continent. Le Président de l’Assemblée législative du peuple (ALP), Ousmane Bougouma, représentant le président du Faso, a reconnu que l'Afrique dispose d'immenses potentialités et d'une jeunesse qui constitue sa première richesse. « Mais, ces atouts ne deviendront une prospérité que si nous levons les obstacles à la circulation des personnes et des marchandises », a-t-il indiqué. Pour lui, les tensions géopolitiques et les perturbations des routes maritimes ont révélé la vulnérabilité des économies face aux chocs extérieurs. Il a confié que la performance logistique ne doit pas se mesurer seulement en coûts et en délais, mais aussi par sa résilience, sa sécurité et sa contribution à la souveraineté. « Pour le Burkina Faso, pays sans littoral, cet enjeu est vital. Chaque rupture de corridor, chaque congestion portuaire, chaque formalité de trop pèse sur le coût des marchandises et sur la compétitivité de nos entreprises », a déploré Ousmané Bougouma. Pilier du développement socio-économique La Directrice générale (DG) du CBC, Denise Bado, a indiqué que le présent symposium traduit une volonté commune à faire face avec lucidité aux chocs multiformes, géopolitiques, sanitaires, énergétiques et économiques qui pèsent sur les systèmes d'approvisionnement. « La fragilité de certaines de nos infrastructures et les défis de coordination des acteurs le long des corridors nous interpellent collectivement sur les contraintes qui affectent la fluidité et la résilience de nos chaînes d'approvisionnement », a signifié Denise Bado. Quant au ministre d’Etat, ministre chargé de la Mobilité, Emile Zerbo, il a souhaité que ce cadre d’échanges contribue à faciliter le transport des marchandises et à rapprocher les populations des différents pays en favorisant leur mobilité. Il a ajouté que cette rencontre constitue une occasion pour les experts de la sous-région de réfléchir à l’accélération de la digitalisation du secteur de la logistique, afin de faciliter les opérations de transport et de transit. Le directeur général du Port autonome de Douala, Cyrus Ngo’o, dont la structure est le sponsor officiel de cette édition, a salué cette initiative qui renforce les liens entre les économies et contribue, aux côtés des partenaires, à une meilleure intégration logistique du continent. Le parrain de Translog Africa 2026, El hadj Souleymane Zidnaba, a souligné que la résilience logistique appelle à une mobilisation collective des pouvoirs publics, des transporteurs, des opérateurs logistiques, des gestionnaires d’infrastructures et des organisations professionnelles. « De notre côté, les entreprises doivent également assumer leur part de responsabilité en investissant dans l’innovation, la digitalisation et l’anticipation des risques, tout en respectant les dispositions du règlement 14 de l’UEMOA », a-t-il promis. Aly SAWADOGO

items.title: 66e anniversaire des Forces armées nationales : un cross populaire pour lancer les festivités
items.description: Les Forces armées nationales ont organisé un cross populaire, placé sous le signe de la cohésion, dans le cadre des activités commémoratives de leur 66e anniversaire, mardi 20 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Dans le cadre de la commémoration de leur 66e anniversaire, les Forces armées nationales (FAN) ont donné le coup d’envoi des activités le mardi 20 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. A cette occasion, un cross populaire a été organisé dans l’après-midi ayant mobilisé des éléments des Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS), des corps paramilitaires et des populations civiles. L’initiative vise à consolider les liens entre les différentes forces engagées dans la défense du territoire national et à renforcer leur proximité avec les populations. Partis de la place de la Révolution, les participants ont suivi un itinéraire passant par le rond-point du 2-Octobre, celui de la Bataille des rails, le CBC, la rue pavée et la station Total, avant de revenir à leur point de départ. Cette endurance a été suivie d’une séance d’aérobic, dans une ambiance marquée par l’effort physique et la convivialité. Présidée par le chef d’Etat-major général des Armées, le général de brigade Moussa Diallo, cette activité sportive a constitué un moment de rassemblement entre les différentes composantes des forces de défense et de sécurité. Le sport au service de la cohésion Pour le commandant de l’Institut de l’enseignement militaire supérieur Tiéfo-Amoro, le colonel-major Céleste Joseph Moussa Coulibaly, ce cross traduit la volonté des forces de défense et de sécurité de manifester leur unité à travers le sport. « Nous sommes des militaires, des forces de défense et de sécurité et le sport fait partie intégrante de nos activités », a-t-il souligné. Il a ajouté que la participation des civils à cette activité témoigne de la cohésion recherchée entre les forces combattantes et les populations. Le colonel-major Céleste Joseph Moussa Coulibaly a également salué la mobilisation enregistrée à Ouagadougou. Il a félicité les participants et exprimé l’espoir de voir le même engouement dans les autres régions militaires. Au-delà de son caractère sportif, le cross populaire porte un message de solidarité face aux défis sécuritaires. Le commandant de l’Institut de l’enseignement militaire supérieur Tiéfo-Amoro a appelé les Burkinabè à rester unis autour des autorités pour lutter contre le terrorisme. « Nous n’avons qu’un seul Burkina Faso », a-t-il rappelé, invitant les forces de défense et de sécurité à demeurer en symbiose pour venir à bout de cette menace. Ce cross populaire marque le début d’une série d’activités prévues dans le cadre du 66e anniversaire des Forces armées nationales. Les manifestations commémoratives vont se poursuivre durant la semaine, avec pour point d’orgue la cérémonie du 1er novembre 2026, qui sera marquée notamment par une prise d’armes et des décorations. Samira Alida KAMBOU

items.title: Journée internationale de la femme rurale : des équipements pour renforcer la résilience des femmes de Yaagda
items.description: La ministre de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kabré, a présidé, le mardi 20 octobre 2026 à Oula, dans la province du Yatenga, la commémoration en différé de la 29e édition de la Journée internationale de la femme rurale. La célébration a été marquée par une remise de matériels technologiques de production à des groupements féminins. Le gouvernement du Burkina Faso reconnait l’importance de l’autonomisation économique des femmes, notamment celles confrontées aux difficultés liées aux déplacements. C’est pourquoi, à l’occasion de la commémoration en différé de la 29e édition de la Journée internationale de la femme rurale à Oula dans la province du Yatenga, le mardi 20 octobre 2026, des matériels technologiques de production ont été remis à 14 groupements féminins de la région de Yaadga. D’une valeur de 16 millions F CFA, le don est composé de six motoculteurs, d’outils de labours, de 21 moto pompes, de 50 arrosoirs, d’un moulin, de trois kits de transformation post-récolte de pommes de terre, de 8 charrettes et des semences. A cela s’ajoute un tracteur et deux tricycles pour soutenir les activités des femmes. Placée sur le thème, « Résilience des populations : quelles stratégies pour un meilleur accès des femmes rurales retournées aux facteurs de production et de transformation », la cérémonie a été présidée par le ministre de la Famille et de la Solidarité, le lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kabré. Pour elle, cette commémoration donne l’occasion de traduire des paroles en actes concrets. « Sous le leadership du camarade capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, notre pays a engagé une Offensive agropastorale et halieutique qui traduit sa volonté de reconquérir notre souveraineté alimentaire. Dans cette dynamique, la femme burkinabè occupe une place déterminante », a-t-elle indiqué. Selon elle, les femmes qui sont présentes dans toutes les étapes de la chaîne agricole constituent une force productive indispensable à la réalisation de cette ambition nationale. Elle a rappelé que le thème de la journée s’inscrit dans les orientations du Plan RELANCE 2026-2030, qui vise à atteindre la souveraineté alimentaire et créer des emplois productifs pour les jeunes et les femmes dans le secteur agro-sylvo-pastoral. Le lieutenant-colonel Passowendé Pélagie Kabré, a insisté sur la bonne utilisation et l’entretien régulier des équipements remis aux femmes, afin qu’elles puissent en tirer durablement profit.Pour les femmes bénéficiaires, ce soutien vient à point nommé. Leur porte-parole, Alizèta Zono, a indiqué que ces moyens représentent un levier potentiel de reprise de leurs activités génératrices de revenus. « Le geste du gouvernement vient renforcer notre capacité à faire face aux difficultés et à retrouver progressivement une place active dans le tissu économique local », a-t-elle rassuré. Elle a traduit sa reconnaissance au gouvernement et au président du Faso qui œuvrent chaque jour pour le bien être de la population et en particulier les femmes. Bassirou BADINI

items.title: Elon Musk and Dario Amodei Are Offering Gifts—With Strings Attached
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Many people are understandably focused on the question of how AI will transform our civilization. Will it cure cancer? Will it end world hunger? Will it hack everyone’s bank accounts and incubate the next pandemic? But those who are already profiting from this technological revolution also have a more immediate concern. Their problem is—to paraphrase one of my favorite lines from Scarface —what to do with all the cash. Over the past few days, two of America’s most prominent AI leaders have offered proposals for returning some of the spoils of the AI boom to the public. On Sunday, Anthropic announced that it would set aside 5 percent of the company’s stock in a new LLC—the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund—to be spent on causes it deems to be in the public’s interest. More stock may be added as the company becomes more valuable. If the company goes public at its current projected valuation of $1.5 trillion , the fund could hold $75 billion, making it one of the largest charities on the planet. (For context, the Gates Foundation Trust had about $89 billion in it at the end of last year.) Elon Musk, a centibillionaire and a longtime skeptic of traditional philanthropy, criticized the move and tried to one-up it, writing on X that he’d be giving one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America.” According to The New York Times ’ back-of-the-napkin math, this could end up being a donation of more than $10 billion. What AI’s biggest winners decide to do with their money could have profound consequences for how Americans live their lives. The birth of modern AI may turn out to be the biggest wealth-creation event in human history, yet most Americans are feeling those effects indirectly . AI is making some people’s jobs easier and driving innovation, but it isn’t hitting everyone’s personal finances equally, and almost half of U.S. adults think the technology will widen the gap between the rich and the poor. Musk and Anthropic are now laying out two different visions for AI-driven philanthropy—raising thorny questions about the level of control that the investor class will exert over our shared future. The first and most obvious question for Anthropic: What if the company’s understanding of the “public good” doesn’t line up with the public’s wants or needs? Anthropic’s leaders, Dario and Daniela Amodei, have already committed to giving away most of their own personal wealth, and Dario has written on his blog about the kinds of philanthropy he admires. The Gates Foundation and PEPFAR, President George W. Bush’s public initiative for global AIDS relief, are both on his list. But how the firm’s leaders will actually decide to apportion these gifts remains somewhat nebulous. A press release for Anthropic’s fund lists “large donations to traditional nonprofits” and “direct distributions to specific populations” as examples of possible projects. Another stated goal is to remediate the effects of a massive, AI-driven labor-market transformation—an ironic instance of a company trying to solve a problem it helped create. As many politicians and even AI corporations themselves have argued, this tech is powerful enough, and potentially such an important part of the global economy, that the wealth it creates may merit some degree of public control. Last October, as one possible plan for reckoning with the economic consequences of AI, Anthropic floated the idea of using “sovereign wealth funds to give citizens stakes in AI revenues.” (OpenAI’s leaders have also reportedly considered giving 5 percent of the company to the government.) At least for now, though, the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund isn’t giving anyone outside of the company a stake. And the fact that it won’t be a 501(c)(3), like the Gates Foundation, means that it won’t have to deal with the kinds of mandatory financial disclosures that are meant to keep charitable organizations maximally transparent. A democratic way to approach this project would be for the government to aggressively tax the company and decide for itself how to spend the money. Not every American agrees with their government representatives’ approach to resource allocation, but at least in the public sector, the people have a voice. Although Musk’s path is also billionaire-led, it gives Americans a much more direct stake. Donald Trump clarified yesterday that Musk’s donation, if it happens, would use the country’s new child-savings accounts (known as “Trump Accounts”) as a vehicle. Rather than earmarking shares for a self-sustaining charitable foundation, Musk would be effectively cutting out the middleman, giving American children a piece of the company that houses his biggest AI bets. It would likely be a smaller total donation than Anthropic’s; one share per child may not turn out to be all that much money in the long run. And Trump Accounts aren’t a perfect dispersal mechanism ; parents can’t reject donated shares, and they can’t immediately sell them. Once account holders turn 18, though, they can spend Musk’s gift on whatever they want. Musk, like other tech billionaires , has questioned traditional modes of philanthropy. He knows that the public knows that giving can be an expression of power and control—a way to rehabilitate a donor’s image or provide political insulation for the donor and his enterprises. Musk may be getting something out of this too. If more people own a little chunk of the AI economy, will they start to become more receptive to data centers and other Big Tech interventions? The donation could also give recipients a reason to be less critical of Musk and his businesses; people with a stake in the company might be more inclined to tolerate unscrupulous behavior. Still, if he can follow through on his approach (and especially if he continues to donate AI stock, as he hinted in his post yesterday), his gift could have a real impact. When SpaceX was about to go public earlier this year, my colleague Matteo Wong observed that “by weaving itself into the finances of most businesses and households in America, the AI industry is quickly making itself too big to fail.” AI is already deeply embedded in our life: in the businesses we interact with, in the pension funds and 401(k)s around which we plan our future. These massive donations, which represent a deviation from tech-industry norms, could reshape society for the better. But if the public comes to rely on Anthropic’s investments or on direct payouts from SpaceX, it’ll need to start caring even more about how well these companies perform . Public welfare needn’t be contingent on the whims of a few powerful firms; so much else already is. Related: Choose your overload—Musk vs. Bezos. Elon Musk is dropping a boulder in a kiddie pool. Today’s News Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg is donating roughly $80 million to support Democrats in the midterm elections, and is focused on helping the party win control of the House. Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee is transferring $50 million to groups supporting Republican House and Senate candidates. The United Kingdom announced that it will deploy Royal Air Force fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to defend against missile and drone attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. The jets will protect Saudi cities and infrastructure but will not conduct offensive strikes inside Yemen, British officials said. Elon Musk ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink service last week, disrupting drone operations and air defenses, according to The Wall Street Journal . Musk reportedly discussed the decision, and President Trump said he did not know who was responsible for the move. He explores the sometimes fatal dangers of this aggressive approach . Explore all of our newsletters here. The cynicism of Trump’s climate policy Elizabeth Bruenig on the woman who has prevented 200 executions Evening Read Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic. Source: Michael Kovac / Getty. Theranos-Style Fraud Has Become the Norm By Idrees Kahloon Perhaps Elizabeth Holmes was simply ahead of her time: Today, the Theranos founder’s crimes look less notorious amid a pervasive culture of grift and graft. Her biotechnology company infamously promised to revolutionize medicine by conducting hundreds of tests on mere pinpricks of blood. A decade after it fell into disgrace, and three years after she began serving her 11-year federal-prison sentence for defrauding investors of hundreds of millions of dollars, Holmes is the subject of a new documentary. You Can See Everything , directed by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, came about because Holmes and her partner, the hotel heir Billy Evans, invited Fielder, a surrealist sketch comedian, to live with them just before she went to prison. They allowed him to film whatever he saw. The result is unsettling, because Holmes’s placid indifference toward the truth has become more familiar than it was when Theranos unraveled.
